chapters.html:
A Complete Beginner-to-University-Level Self-Study Textbook Based on the Supplied Lakehead University Course Material

Prepared for independent learning from first principles.

This book explains the ten supplied sections: 1.1-1.5, 1.7-1.9, and 2.1-2.2. Chapter 0 supplies the prerequisite arithmetic, algebra, notation, and reasoning. Section 1.6 was not supplied and has not been inserted. Original teaching examples and prerequisite explanations are additions by the author; source examples carry PDF page references.

  1. The companion Exercise Workbook contains the supplied exercise pages and numbered worked solutions.

  2. Answers developed here are independently derived teaching solutions.

  3. Where a matching selected solution appears in the supplied course PDF, the workbook records that cross-check.

  4. Neither document claims to be an instructor-issued answer key.

chapters.title: How to use this book independently
chapters.html:
You may open any chapter. If a symbol or an algebraic step is unfamiliar, use Chapter 0 or the glossary. The course section appears in each chapter title so that you can move between this book and your slides without guessing where a topic belongs. There is no timetable or required study duration.

  1. Read a worked example as a chain of decisions.

  2. Before looking at a calculation, identify what the question asks: a solution, an existence decision, a span test, an independence test, an image, a standard matrix, or an inverse.

  3. These requests may use the same row-reduction calculation but require different concluding sentences.

  1. Every significant row operation in the worked reductions is followed by the complete updated matrix.

  2. Read its rows as equations.

  3. The explanations name the unknowns, identify free choices, and verify the answer in the original data.

  4. A calculation is useful only when you can explain what it establishes.

End-of-chapter questions have worked answers in the practice-solutions chapter. The companion workbook supplies course-based practice; the questions in this textbook are original foundation and transfer practice unless explicitly labeled as a course example. You can cover an answer with a sheet of paper, attempt the question, then compare your reasoning. This is optional self-study, not a progress system.

  1. Conventions. All computations here use real numbers and column vectors unless stated otherwise.

  2. A vector written (a,b,c) in a sentence represents the column with those entries.

  3. A superscript T means transpose.

  4. A superscript -1 on a matrix means inverse, not entrywise reciprocal.

  5. A vertical divider in a matrix separates coefficients from appended right-hand sides.

  6. It is not an extra column.

  7. All parameters are real unless a problem says otherwise.

  1. The two questions to keep separate. Existence asks whether a solution is possible.

  2. Uniqueness asks whether two different solutions are possible.

  3. Decide existence first.

  4. An inconsistent system cannot have a unique solution, and the presence of a free coefficient variable does not repair a contradiction.

chapters.title: 0. Mathematical foundations
chapters.html:
1. This chapter is supplementary prerequisite teaching.

  2. It is included because the supplied linear algebra assumes these skills.

  3. None of it adds a later course topic.

0.1 Numbers, variables, and signs

SEE THE IDEA

A sign can name a position or an operation

Start with positions, then read what the operation asks you to do.

Remember. Subtracting a negative means adding its opposite: 4 − (−5) = 9.

A number can describe an amount, a position, or a change. On a number line, 3 is three units to the right of 0 and -3 is three units to the left. The minus sign can name a negative number, as in -3, or describe subtraction, as in 5 - 3. In -(-3), the outer minus asks for the opposite of -3, giving 3.

  1. A variable is a symbol whose value is being discussed.

  2. In

    2x+3=112x + 3 = 11

    , x is unknown;

  3. in

    y=2x+3y = 2x + 3

    , x may be an input and y the corresponding output.

  4. The same letter need not play the same role in every problem.

  5. State what your unknowns represent before calculating an application.

  1. Multiplication by a positive number preserves direction on the number line.

  2. Multiplication by a negative number reverses direction.

  3. Thus

    (−2)(3)=−6,(−2)(−3)=6(-2)(3) = -6, (-2)(-3) = 6

    , and

    2(−3)=−62(-3) = -6

  4. The rule for two negatives follows from distributivity:

    0=(−2)(3+(−3))=−6+(−2)(−3)0 = (-2)(3 + (-3)) = -6 + (-2)(-3)

  5. so the last product must be 6.

  1. Subtraction means adding the opposite.

  2. For example,

    4−(−5)=4+5=94 - (-5) = 4 + 5 = 9

  3. but

    −4−5=−9-4 - 5 = -9

  4. Parentheses are essential in row operations: if an entry is -5 and you subtract twice a row whose corresponding entry is -3, the new entry is

    −5−2(−3)=1-5 - 2(-3) = 1

  1. Worked arithmetic. Evaluate -3 + 2(-4) - (-5).

  2. Multiplication comes first:

    2(−4)=−82(-4) = -8

  3. Replace subtracting -5 by adding 5.

  4. The result is

    −3−8+5=−6-3 - 8 + 5 = -6

  5. Do not turn the entire expression positive because it contains two minus signs;

  6. only the particular subtraction of a negative changes to addition.

0.2 Fractions and exact arithmetic

SEE THE IDEA

Keep the pieces the same size

Before adding fractions, rename them using the same denominator.

  1. 121/2 = 363/6
  2. 131/3 = 262/6
  3. 363/6 + 262/6 = 565/6
(−34)+(56)=(−912)+(1012)=112(-3/4) + (5/6) = (-9/12) + (10/12) = 1/12

Remember. Add numerators after denominators match. Keep exact fractions during elimination.

  1. The fraction a/b means a divided by b, with b nonzero.

  2. Equivalent fractions are formed by multiplying or dividing both numerator and denominator by the same nonzero number.

  3. Thus

    69=236/9 = 2/3

  4. The fraction −23-2/3 equals 2/(-3),

  5. but (-2)/(-3) equals 232/3.

  1. To add fractions, express them with a common denominator.

  2. For 121/2 + 131/3, use sixths:

    36+26=563/6 + 2/6 = 5/6

  3. Adding the denominators would produce 252/5, which is a different number.

  4. For −34-3/4 + 565/6, use twelfths:

    −912+1012=112-9/12 + 10/12 = 1/12

  1. Multiply numerators together and denominators together:

    (23)(−94)=−1812=−32(2/3)(-9/4) = -18/12 = -3/2

  2. Cancel common factors before multiplying if helpful: 9 divided by 3 is 3, and 2 divided by 4 is 121/2.

  3. Cancellation applies to factors, not arbitrary terms in a sum.

  4. You cannot cancel the 2 in (2 + 3)/2 to obtain 1 + 3.

  1. Dividing by a nonzero fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal.

  2. Hence

    (35)27=(35)(72)=2110(3/5)/(2/7) = (3/5)(7/2) = 21/10

  3. Division by 0 is never allowed.

  4. If a row has pivot -3, multiplying the row by −13-1/3 changes that pivot to 1;

  5. every entry of the row must receive the same multiplier.

  1. Worked row arithmetic. If

    R1=[2−35]R₁ = [2, -3, 5]

    and

    R2=[112−2]R₂ = [1, 1/2, -2]

    , then R2R₂ ← R2R₂ - (121/2)R1R₁ gives

    [1−112+32−2−52]=[02−92][1 - 1, 1/2 + 3/2, -2 - 5/2] = [0, 2, -9/2]

  2. The fraction is exact.

  3. A rounded decimal such as -4.5 is harmless here,

  4. but fractions prevent rounding errors from accumulating in longer calculations.

0.3 Expressions, equality, and solving an equation

SEE THE IDEA

An equation is a balance

Apply the same reversible operation to both sides.

  1. 3x − 2 = 10
  2. Add 2: 3x = 12
  3. Divide by 3: x = 4
  4. Check: 3(4) − 2 = 10

Remember. A subscript labels an entry; a power multiplies a quantity by itself.

  1. An expression such as 3x - 2 has a value after x is chosen.

  2. An equation such as

    3x−2=103x - 2 = 10

    asserts that two expressions have equal values.

  3. A solution is a choice that makes the assertion true.

  4. Checking

    x=4x = 4

    gives

    3(4)−2=103(4) - 2 = 10

  5. so 4 is a solution.

  6. Checking

    x=2x = 2

    gives 4 rather than 10,

  7. so 2 is not.

  1. Use the order: grouping, powers, multiplication and division from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right.

  2. For 2 + 3(4 - 1)^2, first obtain

    4−1=34 - 1 = 3

    , then

    32=93^2 = 9

    , then

    3·9=273·9 = 27

    , then

    2+27=292 + 27 = 29

  3. A subscript such as x2x₂ is a label;

  4. it is not a power and does not mean x squared.

  1. Distributivity says

    a(b+c)=ab+a(b + c) = ab +

    ac.

  2. In -2(x - 3), distribute the negative multiplier to both terms: -2x + 6.

  3. Combining like terms gives

    3x+2x=5x3x + 2x = 5x

  4. but 3x + 2y cannot be combined unless x and y are known to be equal.

  1. To solve an equation, preserve its truth by performing the same reversible action on both sides.

  2. Starting with

    3x−2=103x - 2 = 10

    , add 2 to both sides to get

    3x=123x = 12

  3. divide both sides by 3 to get

    x=4x = 4

  4. The phrase 'move -2 to the other side' abbreviates adding 2 to both sides.

  5. It is not a separate rule that lets terms cross an equals sign without a reason.

  1. Worked fraction equation. Solve

    x3−2=56x/3 - 2 = 5/6

  2. Add

    2=1262 = 12/6

    to both sides:

    x3=176x/3 = 17/6

  3. Multiply both sides by 3:

    x=172x = 17/2

  4. Check:

    (172)3−2=176−126=56(17/2)/3 - 2 = 17/6 - 12/6 = 5/6

  5. The check uses the original equation and therefore catches a sign error made during rearrangement.

  1. Two warnings matter later.

  2. Multiplying an equation by zero loses information:

    x=4x = 4

    would become

    0=00 = 0

    , which is true for every x.

  3. Dividing by a variable may discard solutions if that variable could be zero.

  4. Row scaling therefore uses a known nonzero number, and parameter problems require a separate case when a potential pivot becomes zero.

0.4 Substitution and simultaneous equations

SEE THE IDEA

A system means “all at once”

One pair must make every original equation true.

Candidatex + y = 5x − y = 1
(3,2)3 + 2 = 5 ✓3 − 2 = 1 ✓
(1,4)1 + 4 = 5 ✓1 − 4 = −3 ✗

Remember. Checking only one equation is insufficient.

  1. Substitution means replacing a symbol by its stated value or expression wherever that symbol occurs.

  2. If

    x=2t−1x = 2t - 1

    , then 3x + 4 becomes

    3(2t−1)+4=6t+13(2t - 1) + 4 = 6t + 1

  3. Keep parentheses around the replacement until you have distributed correctly.

  1. A system asks you to satisfy several equations at the same time.

  2. Consider

    x+y=5x + y = 5

    and

    x−y=1x - y = 1

  3. Adding the equations gives

    2x=62x = 6

  4. so

    x=3x = 3

  5. Substitute into the first equation:

    3+y=53 + y = 5

  6. hence

    y=2y = 2

  7. Both original equations check:

    3+2=53 + 2 = 5

    and

    3−2=13 - 2 = 1

  8. Satisfying only the first equation would be insufficient;

  9. (1,4) fails the second.

  1. If the system instead says

    x+y=5x + y = 5

    and

    x+y=7x + y = 7

    , subtracting the first equation from the second gives

    0=20 = 2

  2. This cannot be true,

  3. so no pair works.

  4. If the second equation is

    2x+2y=102x + 2y = 10

    , it repeats the first equation.

  5. Every pair (5 - t,t) works, because

    (5−t)+t=5(5 - t) + t = 5

  6. A repeated equation supplies no new restriction.

0.5 Coordinates and lines

SEE THE IDEA

A solution is a shared point

The graphs visualize the same “all equations at once” requirement.

The horizontal axis is the x1x₁-axis and the vertical axis is the x2x₂-axis. Their intersection is the origin (0,0). An ordered pair (a,b) means move a units horizontally, then b units vertically. The order matters: (2,-1) and (-1,2) are different points. Three coordinates locate a point in three-dimensional space.

  1. The graph of an equation is the set of all points satisfying it.

  2. For

    x2=2x1+1x₂ = 2x₁ + 1

    , choosing

    x1=0,1,2x₁ = 0,1,2

    gives points (0,1), (1,3), (2,5).

  3. The line passes through all of them.

  4. Its slope 2 means a horizontal change of 1 produces a vertical change of 2.

  5. A vertical line such as

    x1=3x₁ = 3

    cannot be written as x2x₂ = mx1x₁ + c,

  6. but it is still a linear equation.

  1. An equation ax1x₁ + bx

    ₂=c₂ = c

    with at least one of a,b nonzero describes a line in the plane.

  2. Two such lines can intersect once, be distinct and parallel, or coincide.

  3. Those pictures correspond to one solution, no solutions, and infinitely many solutions of a two-equation system.

  4. Equations in three variables normally describe planes;

  5. the common solution must lie in all the specified planes.

The diagrams show the three possibilities for two genuine lines in the plane. A system with more equations still demands a point common to every graph, not merely an intersection of two selected graphs.

0.6 Reading mathematical language

SEE THE IDEA

Read the logical direction

“If” and “if and only if” ask for different arguments.

NotationMeaningProof needed
P ⇒ QP guarantees QOne direction
P ⇔ QEach guarantees the otherBoth directions
∅ versus {0}No members versus one zero memberDifferent sets

  1. The symbol ℝ names the real numbers.

  2. The statement

    t∈ℝt ∈ ℝ

    means t is a real number.

  3. A set is a collection of objects;

  4. braces list its members.

  5. The empty set, ∅, has no members.

  6. The set {0} contains one member, zero,

  7. so it is different from ∅.

  8. In linear algebra, the zero in {0} may be a vector, whose size is determined by the context.

  1. The statement

    P⇒QP ⇒ Q

    means 'if P is true, then Q is true.' It does not automatically assert the reverse.

  2. The statement

    P⇔QP ⇔ Q

    means both directions: P implies Q and Q implies P.

  3. It is read 'P if and only if Q.' To prove an equivalence, explain both directions or give a chain of already established equivalences.

  1. A universal statement says something about every allowed object.

  2. For instance, 'every homogeneous system has a solution' includes systems of every permitted size.

  3. One numerical example cannot prove it.

  4. The vector

    x=0x = 0

    supplies a solution for an arbitrary matrix A, which is a general argument.

  5. A false universal statement can be disproved by a single counterexample satisfying its assumptions and violating its conclusion.

  1. A theorem is a mathematical statement proved from definitions and accepted earlier results.

  2. Its assumptions matter. 'A consistent system with a free variable has infinitely many solutions' includes the assumption of consistency.

  3. Omitting that assumption makes the statement false.

  4. A proof is a chain of justified statements that begins with the assumptions and ends with the desired conclusion.

  5. An intuitive picture helps explain a theorem,

  6. but a proof must cover every case covered by its wording.

  1. Sigma notation is a compact way to add indexed terms.

  2. The expression Σ from

    j=1j=1

    to n of aja_j xjx_j means a1a₁x1x₁ + a2a₂x2x₂ + ... + ana_n xnx_n.

  3. The index j runs through the indicated labels.

  4. No new operation is involved.

  5. We use expanded sums whenever they make a new idea easier to read.

0.7 Foundation practice

TRY IT YOURSELF · F1

F1. Evaluate -2(3 - 5) + 121/2 - 565/6 exactly.

Show Detailed Solution · F1

F1.

Work inside the parentheses first

3−5=−23 - 5 = -2

The minus sign means move five units left from 3. The result is negative.

Multiply by the outside −2

(−2)(−2)=4(-2)(-2) = 4

A negative times a negative is positive. The outside −2 multiplies the entire parenthesis.

Give the fractions a common denominator

12=361/2 = 3/6
12−56=36−56=−26=−131/2 - 5/6 = 3/6 - 5/6 = -2/6 = -1/3

Sixths have the same size, so subtract their numerators. Divide numerator and denominator by 2 to simplify.

Combine the integer and the fraction

4−13=123−13=1134 - 1/3 = 12/3 - 1/3 = 11/3
FINAL ANSWER
11311/3
TRY IT YOURSELF · F2

F2. Solve 2(x - 3)/5 = 4 and verify your answer.

Show Detailed Solution · F2

F2.

Start with the given equation

2(x−3)5=42(x - 3)/5 = 4

The fraction applies to all of 2(x − 3), not just to the 3.

Undo division by 5

5(2(x−3)5)=5(4)5(2(x - 3)/5) = 5(4)
2(x−3)=202(x - 3) = 20

Multiply both sides by the same nonzero number to preserve equality.

Undo multiplication by 2

2(x−3)2=2022(x - 3)/2 = 20/2
x−3=10x - 3 = 10

Undo subtraction of 3

x−3+3=10+3x - 3 + 3 = 10 + 3
x=13x = 13

Check in the original equation

2(13−3)5=2(10)5=205=42(13 - 3)/5 = 2(10)/5 = 20/5 = 4
FINAL ANSWER
x=13x = 13
TRY IT YOURSELF · F3

F3. Solve x + 2y = 7 and 3x - y = 7. Explain why both equations must be checked.

Show Detailed Solution · F3

F3 and S11.

F3 and S11. The same system appears twice so that you can compare the substitution and matrix methods. Here is the complete matrix solution; the answer must satisfy both original equations.

  1. Each coefficient column corresponds to one unknown;

  2. the column after the vertical divider records the right-hand sides.

  3. We use reversible row operations to reveal the constraints.

The starting matrix is:

    x1=3x_1 = 3

  2. so no arbitrary choices remain.

Verification in the original equations. For p, the left-hand sides A p are:

These entries equal the original right-hand sides, in order.

What does the reduced matrix say?

[103012]

There are 2 equations and 2 unknown weights or coordinates. The divider separates the constants from those unknowns.

Separate determined coordinates from free choices

CoordinateLook at its columnWhat you may do
x1x_1Pivot column → basicDetermined by its pivot equation

Determine x1 from its row

Determine x2 from its row

x2=2x_2 = 2

Subtract each free-variable term from both sides. The pivot coefficient is 1, so no further division is needed.

Verify the starting point in every original equation

Every coordinate is fixed. There are no free choices, so the solution is unique.

TRY IT YOURSELF · F4

F4. Explain the difference between x2x₂ and x2x^2, and between 'there exists a solution' and 'there exists exactly one solution.'

Show Detailed Solution · F4

F4.

A subscript is a label

x2x_2

This means the unknown labeled 2. It does not tell you to multiply x by 2 or square it.

A superscript can be a power

x2=xxx^2 = x x

This means multiply x by itself. If x = 3, the result is 9.

Existence and uniqueness ask different questions

QuestionWhat must be true
Does a solution exist?At least one input satisfies every equation.
Is the solution unique?One input works, and no different input works.

A whole line of solutions has many inputs, so existence holds but uniqueness fails.

FINAL ANSWER

A label and a power have different meanings. Having a solution and having exactly one solution are different claims.

TRY IT YOURSELF · F5

F5. Disprove: 'If two equations have one common solution, they have the same solution set.' Supply actual equations and explain their different sets.

Show Detailed Solution · F5

F5.

Choose equations with one shared point

x+y=1x + y = 1
x−y=1x - y = 1

Check the shared point (1,0)

1+0=11 + 0 = 1
1−0=11 - 0 = 1

It satisfies both equations.

Find a point that belongs to only one equation

0+1=10 + 1 = 1
0−1=−10 - 1 = -1

The point (0,1) satisfies the first equation and fails the second. The two solution sets therefore differ.

FINAL ANSWER

The statement is false. One shared point does not mean two sets contain exactly the same points.

Worked answers appear in Chapter 12.

chapters.title: 1. Section 1.1 - Systems of linear equations
chapters.html:
Source correspondence: Combined PDF pages 1-11; exercise PDF pages 1-2. This chapter expands the lecture definitions and the two principal elimination examples.

1.1 What makes an equation linear?

SEE THE IDEA

Linear means no interaction between unknowns

Unknowns occur only to the first power, multiplied by fixed coefficients.

LinearNot linear in x,yReason
2x − 3y = 7xy = 7Product of unknowns
x + y = 1x2x² + y = 1An unknown is squared
0x + y = 21/x + y = 2An unknown is in a denominator

  1. The equation

    2x1−3x2+x3=72x₁ - 3x₂ + x₃ = 7

    gives a weighted sum of unknown entries.

  2. The numbers 2,-3,1 are coefficients; 7 is the constant on the right.

  3. A missing variable has coefficient 0.

  4. The general form is a1a₁x1x₁ + ...

    +anxn=b+ a_n x_n = b

    , where the coefficients and b are fixed numbers.

  5. The unknowns appear to the first power and are not multiplied together.

  1. Thus

    x1+2x2=3x₁ + 2x₂ = 3

    is linear;

  2. x1x2=3,x12+x2=1x₁x₂ = 3, x₁^2 + x₂ = 1

    , and

    1x1+x2=41/x₁ + x₂ = 4

    are not linear equations in these variables.

  3. A coefficient can be a fraction or a square root if it is a fixed number.

  4. The restriction concerns how the unknowns enter, not how simple the known coefficients look.

  1. A solution is a list of numbers in the variable order that makes every equation true.

  2. The solution set contains every such list.

  3. Two systems are equivalent when their solution sets are identical.

  4. A consistent system has at least one solution;

  5. an inconsistent one has none.

  6. A linear system over ℝ has zero, one, or infinitely many solutions.

  7. It cannot have exactly two: if p and q are distinct solutions, linearity shows that p + t(q - p) is a solution for every real t.

1.2 Matrices record the equations without changing them

SEE THE IDEA

A matrix is a tidy record of equations

Each row records one equation. Coefficient columns keep the same variable order.

x1+2x2=7x_1 + 2x_2 = 7
3x1−x2=73x_1 - x_2 = 7

  1. A matrix is a rectangular array.

  2. Its size is rows × columns, with rows first.

  3. The coefficient matrix records the coefficients in a fixed variable order.

  4. The augmented matrix appends the constants.

  5. For the lecture system, the coefficient rows are [1−21][1,-2,1], [02−8][0,2,-8], [−459][-4,5,9], and the constants are [08−9][0,8,-9].

  6. The 0 at the start of the second row means the equation has no x1x₁ term.

  7. It is needed to keep the other coefficients in their correct columns.

  1. The coefficient matrix has size 3 × 3.

1.3 Why row operations preserve solutions

SEE THE IDEA

A legal row operation has an undo

Changing equations preserves their solutions when the change can be reversed.

OperationUndo
R2R₂ ← R2R₂ − 3R1R₁R2R₂ ← R2R₂ + 3R1R₁
R1R₁ ← 2R1R₁R1R₁ ← (121/2)R1R₁
R1R₁ ↔ R2R₂Swap again
R1R₁ ← 0R1R₁No undo: information was erased

  1. Three elementary operations are allowed.

  2. Interchange two rows.

  3. Multiply one row by a nonzero scalar.

  4. Replace one row by itself plus a multiple of a different row.

  5. The notation R3R₃ ← R3R₃ + 4R1R₁ means compute four times every entry of row 1, add those entries to row 3, and put the results into row 3.

  6. The arrow describes replacement, not an equation between row numbers.

  1. Interchanging equations changes only their order.

  2. Scaling by

    c≠0c ≠ 0

    is reversible by scaling by 1/c.

  3. Replacing equation E3E₃ by E3E₃ + 4E1E₁ is reversible by subtracting 4E1E₁.

  4. If a list satisfies the original equations, it satisfies the replacement;

  5. if it satisfies the new equations, reversal shows it satisfies the original ones.

  6. This explains preservation in both directions.

  1. Scaling by 0 is not an elementary operation.

  2. Replacing R3R₃ by R3R₃ + 4R1R₁ must change the appended constant as well as every coefficient.

  3. Performing unrelated column operations generally changes which variable combinations are being represented and is not the solving method used here.

1.6 Choosing a method and writing the conclusion

SEE THE IDEA

Decide before doing extra arithmetic

The wording tells you whether you need a decision, one input, or the full set.

Asked forStop when you have
ConsistencyA contradiction or a valid existence argument
Unique solutionConsistency and no free variables
Solve completelyEvery unknown described, including all parameters

  1. Gaussian elimination means using row operations to reach a staircase arrangement, then substituting backward.

  2. Gauss-Jordan elimination continues until each pivot is 1 and its column is otherwise zero.

  3. Both methods preserve the solution set.

  4. The latter makes parameters especially easy to read.

  1. If the question asks whether a solution exists, a consistent echelon form is enough.

  2. If it asks to solve, provide every solution, including arbitrary parameters when appropriate.

  3. If it asks for an intersection, give the point or describe the common set in the original coordinate language.

  4. If it asks to verify, substitute into the original equations;

  5. merely repeating a reduction is not the same check.

  1. Common mistakes. Keeping only equations that are easy to satisfy can lose a contradiction.

  2. Forgetting a zero coefficient shifts columns.

  3. Adding rows without replacing a specified row makes the next step ambiguous.

  4. Multiplying one entry instead of the whole row changes the equations incorrectly.

  5. Always write the chosen operation and then the entire updated matrix.

2.1 The staircase and the pivots

SEE THE IDEA

1 · What is a leading entry?

Read a row from left to right. Skip the zeros. The first number that remains is its leading entry.

The leading entry of a nonzero row is its first nonzero entry when read from left to right.

SEE THE IDEA

2 · REF: build a staircase

Look down the rows: each next leading entry takes a step to the right.

REF checkWhat to look for
Zero rows lastThe completely zero row is below the nonzero rows.
Move rightLeading entries are in columns 1, then 2.
Clear belowAll entries below each leading entry are zero.

A matrix is in row echelon form (REF) when all zero rows are at the bottom, each leading entry is strictly to the right of the leading entry in the row above, and every entry below a leading entry is zero. Leading entries need not be 1 in REF.

SEE THE IDEA

3 · RREF: finish cleaning each pivot column

REF gives the shape. RREF also normalizes each leading entry and clears above it.

6 · Why can there be only one RREF?

Different legal routes can simplify the same constraints. A fully reduced matrix records those constraints in one fixed form.

  1. The supplied uniqueness theorem states that every matrix has exactly one RREF among its row-equivalent matrices.

  2. REF is not unique, because multiplying a nonzero row by 2 may preserve its staircase shape.

  3. The RREF conditions remove that scaling freedom and all entries above pivots.

  4. More deeply, row equivalence preserves all constraints, and RREF is a canonical way to record which earliest variables are determined by later ones.

  5. The following supplementary proof explains that uniqueness rather than trying to establish it by numerical examples.

Deeper Mathematical Explanation · Explore the Full Proof
SEE THE IDEA

The proof in three connections

Follow the logical connections; each arrow needs a reason.

  1. Row operations preserve row span
  2. The row span determines pivot-column indices
  3. Matching pivot coordinates force corresponding rows to agree

Why two different RREF answers cannot both be right

  1. We need one temporary piece of vocabulary.

  2. The row span of a matrix means all linear combinations of its rows, treated as horizontal lists.

  3. This is the same weighted-sum idea used for column vectors later in Section 1.3.

  4. Row operations do not change the row span.

  5. A new row is a combination of old rows,

  6. so every new-row combination is an old-row combination.

  7. Reversibility gives the opposite inclusion.

  8. Therefore row-equivalent matrices have exactly the same row span.

  1. Suppose R and S are two RREF matrices obtained from one matrix.

  2. They have the same row span.

  3. In an RREF matrix, take any nonzero combination of its nonzero rows, and find the first row in the combination whose weight is nonzero.

  4. Its leading pivot is the first nonzero coordinate of the resulting list: all earlier row weights are zero, and all later rows are zero to the left of their own later pivots.

  5. Consequently the possible first-nonzero coordinate locations of vectors in the row span are precisely the pivot-column indices.

  6. Since R and S have the same row span, they have the same pivot columns, in the same order.

  1. Now compare row i of R with row i of S.

  2. Their entries in every common pivot column agree: both have 1 at their own pivot and 0 at the other pivots.

  3. Their difference is in the common row span and is zero at every pivot coordinate.

  4. But any row combination in R has, in pivot column j, exactly the weight on the corresponding pivot row: the pivot columns are identity columns.

  5. If all those coordinates are zero, every row weight is zero,

  6. so the entire combination is zero.

  7. Thus the difference between the two compared rows must be zero.

  8. All corresponding nonzero rows agree, and both matrices place their remaining zero rows at the bottom.

  9. Hence

    R=SR = S

  10. This proves uniqueness while allowing different intermediate operations and different ordinary echelon forms.

2.2 The forward and backward phases

SEE THE IDEA

Two passes, two purposes

The forward phase creates the staircase; the backward phase cleans above the pivots.

Forward → REF

Backward → RREF

  1. Start at the leftmost column containing a possible nonzero pivot.

  2. Interchange rows if needed.

  3. Use a nonzero pivot to clear entries below it.

  4. Move down one row and right to the next possible pivot column.

  5. Continue to REF.

  6. This is the forward phase.

  7. If a column has no available nonzero entry below the previous pivots, skip it;

  8. do not force a pivot there.

  1. For the backward phase, start at the rightmost pivot, scale its row to make the pivot 1, and clear entries above it.

  2. Continue upward and leftward.

  3. Normalizing a pivot earlier, as many examples here do, is also valid.

  4. Arithmetic convenience determines the order;

  5. preserving the equations determines validity.

2.7 Existence and uniqueness theorem

SEE THE IDEA

Existence first. Uniqueness second.

Use two separate decisions, in that order.

  1. Is there an echelon row [0 … 0 | c], c ≠ 0?
  2. Yes: no solution. No: the system is consistent.
  3. If consistent, are any coefficient variables free?
  4. None: unique. At least one: infinitely many.

  1. Theorem (supplied Theorem 2). A linear system is consistent if and only if the last column of its augmented matrix is not a pivot column.

  2. Equivalently, no echelon row is [0...0c][0,...,0 | c] with

    c≠0c ≠ 0

  3. Once consistency is established, the solution is unique exactly when there are no free coefficient variables;

  4. it is infinite exactly when there is at least one free coefficient variable.

  1. Why does the theorem work?

  2. A last-column pivot corresponds to an impossible equation.

  3. Without such a row, free variables can be assigned values and the pivot equations can be solved backward, which constructs a solution.

  4. With no free variables the construction has no arbitrary choices.

  5. With a free variable, changing that coordinate changes the solution itself,

  6. so infinitely many solutions result.

  1. A zero coefficient row does not by itself prove either inconsistency or infinitely many solutions.

  2. Its constant determines whether it is a contradiction.

  3. The number of nonzero coefficient pivots relative to the number of unknowns determines whether free variables remain.

TRY IT YOURSELF · R3

R3R_3. A 3 × 5 coefficient matrix has three pivots. Is Ax = b solvable for every b ∈ ℝ3ℝ^3? Can a consistent system have a unique solution? Distinguish the two conclusions.

Existence: every output row

  1. 3 equations → 3 rows
  2. 3 pivots → a pivot in every row
  3. Every b ∈ ℝ3ℝ³ is attainable

Uniqueness: every input column

  1. 5 unknowns → 5 columns
  2. 5 − 3 = 2 free variables
  3. No consistent system has a unique solution

R3R_3.

Read the dimensions

A 3 × 5 coefficient matrix records 3 equations in 5 unknowns. The right-hand-side vector b has 3 entries.

Ask about existence: inspect rows

There are 3 pivots distributed among 3 rows.

Pivots occupy different rows. Three pivots among three rows therefore give a pivot in every row. There is no unused coefficient row that could turn into 0 = a nonzero constant.

Apply the existence theorem

Ax=bA x = b

A pivot in every coefficient row means this equation can be solved for every three-entry b.

Ask about uniqueness: inspect columns

5−3=25 - 3 = 2

Five unknowns but only three pivot columns leave two free variables. They can vary independently; the pivot equations determine the other unknowns.

FINAL ANSWER

Every b in ℝ3ℝ³ has a solution. Every such system has infinitely many solutions, with two free parameters; none has a unique solution.

Source correspondence: Combined PDF pages 28-36; exercise PDF pages 5-6. Applications include mine outputs and a coal-burning plant.

3.1 A vector keeps several quantities together

SEE THE IDEA

A vector keeps ordered quantities together

Its entries are coordinates in a fixed order; its dimension counts those entries.

  1. A vector is an ordered list of entries, normally written as a column.

  2. The vector (2,-1) can represent a point, a displacement, or two measured quantities.

  3. Its interpretation comes from the problem.

  4. The set ℝ2ℝ^2 contains every column with two real entries; ℝ3ℝ^3 contains every column with three.

  5. In ℝnℝ^n, n is the number of entries, not the numerical size of an entry.

  1. The vector (2,-1) can be drawn as an arrow from (0,0) to (2,-1).

  2. Moving the arrow without changing its length or direction gives the same displacement.

  3. The coordinate point is the endpoint when the arrow starts at the origin.

  4. A vector is not merely its length: (2,0) and (0,2) point in different directions.

  1. Two vectors are equal when they have the same number of entries and their corresponding entries are equal.

  2. Addition is entrywise and needs matching sizes.

  3. For

    u=(2,−1),v=(−3,4),u+v=(2−3,−1+4)=(−1,3)u = (2,-1), v = (-3,4), u + v = (2 - 3,-1 + 4) = (-1,3)

  4. Subtraction is addition of the opposite:

    u−v=(2+3,−1−4)=(5,−5)u - v = (2 + 3,-1 - 4) = (5,-5)

  1. A scalar is an ordinary number multiplying a vector.

  2. The scalar multiple cu multiplies every entry of u by c.

  3. For

    c=−2,−2u=(−4,2)c = -2, -2u = (-4,2)

    : the direction reverses and the length doubles.

  4. The zero vector has every entry zero;

  5. its size must match the surrounding calculation.

  6. Multiplication by 0 produces that vector.

  1. The left diagram adds

    u=(2,1)u = (2,1)

    and

    v=(1,2)v = (1,2)

  2. Starting at the endpoint of u and drawing a copy of v reaches

    u+v=(3,3)u + v = (3,3)

  3. The opposite order reaches the same point.

  4. Completing the parallelogram supplies the geometric version of commutativity.

  5. The right diagram compares u, -u, and 2u.

3.2 Vector algebra has familiar rules

SEE THE IDEA

Add matching coordinates

An arrow picture and coordinate arithmetic describe the same operation.

  1. For vectors of the same size,

    u+v=v+uu + v = v + u

    and

    (u+v)+w=u+(v+w)(u + v) + w = u + (v + w)

  2. Also

    u+0=uu + 0 = u

    and

    u+(−u)=0u + (-u) = 0

  3. Scalars distribute:

    c(u+v)=cu+cvc(u + v) = cu + cv

    and

    (c+d)u=cu+du(c + d)u = cu + du

  4. Scalar multiplication associates:

    c(du)=(cd)uc(du) = (cd)u

    , and

    1u=u1u = u

  5. Each statement follows entry by entry from the corresponding real-number property.

  1. A useful proof illustrates this.

  2. Entry i of c(u + v) is c(uiu_i + viv_i).

  3. Real-number distributivity makes this cuiu_i + cviv_i, which is entry i of cu + cv.

  4. Both vectors have the same size and agree in every entry,

  5. so they are equal.

  6. Checking only the first entry would not prove vector equality in general.

3.3 Linear combinations and unknown weights

SEE THE IDEA

Weights are the unknowns

A linear combination asks how much of each direction is needed.

2(1,0)+3(0,1)=(2,3)2(1,0) + 3(0,1) = (2,3)
  1. Put the given vectors into columns
  2. Use the target as the appended column
  3. Solve for the weights

Remember. A solution to [A | b] gives the combination coefficients.

  1. A linear combination of v1v₁,...,vpv_p is c1c₁v1v₁ + ... + cpc_pvpv_p, where the weights cic_i are scalars.

  2. The weights may be negative or zero.

  3. You are choosing how much of each available vector to use.

3.4 Span is the entire collection of obtainable outputs

SEE THE IDEA

A span is everything the generators can reach

One example is a member; the span is the entire collection of weighted sums.

Remember. Two vectors span a genuine plane only when they are independent.

  5. Two such vectors in ℝ2ℝ^2 span the entire coordinate plane.

4.1 Multiplication combines columns

SEE THE IDEA

Ax is a weighted sum of columns

Each input entry weights the column in the same position.

A(3,2)=3(2,1)+2(−1,3)=(4,9)A(3,2) = 3(2,1) + 2(-1,3) = (4,9)

  1. If A has m rows and n columns and x has n entries, Ax is the vector formed by using the entries of x as weights on the columns of A.

  2. Its size is m × 1.

  3. Thus an m × n matrix takes an input in ℝnℝ^n and produces an output in ℝmℝ^m.

  4. The number of columns must match the number of input entries.

  1. Write A = [a1a₁ ... ana_n].

  2. Then

    Ax=x1a1+Ax = x₁a₁ +

    ... + xnx_n ana_n.

  3. This definition explains the multiplication: every column is a possible output contribution, and the input tells us how to combine them.

  4. An m × n matrix multiplied by an input with m entries is not automatically valid;

  5. check n, not m.

  1. The row computation rule follows by examining one entry.

  2. Entry i of Ax is ai1a_{i1}x1x₁ + ... + ain a_{in}xnx_n.

  3. Multiply matching entries across row i of A and down x, then add.

  4. This sum of products is sometimes called a dot product here.

  5. It is a scalar;

  6. the collection of m such scalars is the output vector.

4.2 Worked product using both views

SEE THE IDEA

Two views give the same output

Compute by columns or by row–column products; the coordinates must agree.

Choose one row

Choose one column

The entries of x are weights. Weight 1 multiplies column 1 of A, weight 2 multiplies column 2, and so on. A negative weight reverses the sign of every entry in that column.

4.3 One problem, three equivalent languages

1 · Start with the two equations

x1+2x2−x3=4x_1 + 2x_2 - x_3 = 4
−5x2+3x3=1-5x_2 + 3x_3 = 1

We seek three numbers that make both equations true at the same time. At this stage we are changing notation, not finding their values.

2 · Identify the three unknowns

x1,x2,x3x_1, x_2, x_3

The subscripts 1, 2, and 3 are labels distinguishing three unknown values. They are not powers or multiplication instructions.

3 · Read one coefficient for every variable

Equationx1x₁x2x₂x3x₃Right side
First12−14
Second0−531

A coefficient is the number multiplying an unknown. The second equation has no x1x₁ term, so its x1x₁ coefficient is 0. The term −x3x₃ means (−1)x3x₃.

4 · Build A from the coefficient rows

Row 1 records the first equation. Row 2 records the second. Keep the variable order x1x₁,x2x₂,x3x₃ in both rows. The constants do not belong in A.

5 · Put the unknowns in a column

x=[x1x2x3]x = [x_1;x_2;x_3]

The unknown vector has size 3 × 1. Its order matches the three columns of A.

6 · Put the constants in a separate column

b=[41]b = [4;1]

This vector has size 2 × 1. Its entries follow the order of the two equations.

7 · Write the full matrix equation

[12−10−53][x1x2x3]=[41][1,2,-1;0,-5,3][x_1;x_2;x_3] = [4;1]
Ax=bA x = b

The sizes (2 × 3)(3 × 1) produce a 2 × 1 output, matching b.

8 · Read the same multiplication by columns

x1[10]+x2[2−5]+x3[−13]=[41]x_1[1;0] + x_2[2;-5] + x_3[-1;3] = [4;1]

The first column carries the x1x₁ coefficients; multiply that entire column by x1x₁. Do the same for columns 2 and 3, with weights x2x₂ and x3x₃. Add matching coordinates.

9 · Expand the weighted columns to recover the system

[x10]+[2x2−5x2]+[−x33x3]=[41][x_1;0] + [2x_2;-5x_2] + [-x_3;3x_3] = [4;1]
x1+2x2−x3=4x_1 + 2x_2 - x_3 = 4
0x1−5x2+3x3=10x_1 - 5x_2 + 3x_3 = 1

Matching first coordinates gives equation 1. Matching second coordinates gives equation 2. Every entry has returned to its original place.

FINAL ANSWER

Linear system ↔ vector equation ↔ matrix equation: the unknowns and constraints are identical. Converting between these representations does not solve the system.

Remember. The row-pivot theorem applies to the coefficient matrix A.

  1. Theorem (supplied Theorem 4). For an m × n matrix A, the following four statements are equivalent:

5.1 Homogeneous means zero right-hand side

SEE THE IDEA

Zero is always a starting solution

With right-hand side zero, the all-zero input always works. The real question is whether anything else works.

A0=0A0 = 0

  1. A homogeneous system has the form

    Ax=0Ax = 0

  2. Its zero on the right is the zero vector in ℝmℝ^m if A is m × n.

  3. Its unknown x lies in ℝnℝ^n.

  4. The choice

    x=0x = 0

    always works, because multiplying every column by weight zero gives zero.

  5. This is the trivial solution.

  6. A nontrivial solution is any solution vector with at least one nonzero entry;

  7. it need not have every entry nonzero.

  1. A homogeneous system has a nontrivial solution if and only if at least one coefficient variable is free.

  2. There is never a contradiction, because the appended zero column stays zero under row operations.

  3. If every variable is basic, the pivot equations force every variable to zero.

  4. If some variable is free, set it to 1 and the other free variables to 0;

  5. the resulting solution is nonzero.

  6. This proves both directions.

TRY IT YOURSELF · H3

H3. If Ap = b and Aq = b, prove that p - q is a homogeneous solution. Explain what this says when Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution.

Show Detailed Solution · H3

H3.

Given: two inputs produce the same b

Ap=bAp = b
Aq=bAq = b

We must show that their difference produces zero. A homogeneous equation has zero on the right.

Apply distributivity

A(p−q)=Ap−AqA(p - q) = Ap - Aq

A acts on the subtraction coordinate by coordinate.

Substitute the two known outputs

Ap−Aq=b−b=0Ap - Aq = b - b = 0

Use the extra hypothesis if only zero is homogeneous

A(p−q)=0A(p-q) = 0
p−q=0p - q = 0
p=qp = q

Under that hypothesis the difference cannot be any nonzero vector.

FINAL ANSWER

The difference p − q is a homogeneous solution. If the homogeneous equation has only zero, any two solutions of Ax = b coincide; every consistent system then has exactly one solution.

6.1 Redundancy and the precise definition

SEE THE IDEA

A redundant direction adds no new reach

Dependence means a nonzero choice of weights can cancel to zero.

2(1,2)−(2,4)=(0,0)2(1,2) - (2,4) = (0,0)

Remember. The all-zero choice of weights proves nothing about dependence.

  1. Imagine assembling outputs from a collection of vectors.

  2. If one vector can already be constructed from the others, including it does not enlarge the span.

  3. It is redundant.

  4. Linear dependence is the algebraic way of detecting such redundancy, including cases that are hard to see geometrically.

  1. Definition. The indexed collection v1v₁,...,vpv_p is linearly independent when c1c₁v1v₁ + ... + cpc_pv

    _p=0_p = 0

    forces c1c₁ = ...

    =cp=0= c_p = 0

  2. It is linearly dependent when at least one choice of weights, not all zero, gives the zero vector.

  3. Such a choice is a dependence relation. 'Not all zero' means at least one weight is nonzero, not that every weight must be nonzero.

  1. Every collection admits the zero-weight combination.

  2. Therefore the fact that

    Ax=0Ax = 0

    has a solution proves nothing about independence: it always does.

  3. The test asks whether it has only that trivial solution.

  4. Put the vectors into columns of A, solve

    Ax=0Ax = 0

    , and look for free variables.

  5. Every column pivot means independent.

  6. A free weight means dependent.

  1. Two nonzero vectors along one line are dependent.

  2. Two vectors in the plane that point along different lines through zero are independent.

  3. Three vectors in ℝ3ℝ^3 may be independent or may lie in a common plane through zero;

  4. a picture alone should not replace a calculation when exact coordinates are available.

SEE THE IDEA

TRY IT YOURSELF · I3

I3. Prove that a subset of an independent collection is independent. Explain why a superset of a dependent collection is dependent.

Show Detailed Solution · I3

I3.

First claim: take a subset of an independent collection

Suppose a weighted sum of the subset vectors is zero. Assign weight 0 to every vector omitted from the full collection. The extended sum is still zero.

Apply independence of the full collection

Its only zero-producing weights are all zero. In particular, the original subset weights must all be zero. That is exactly independence of the subset.

Second claim: enlarge a dependent collection

Start with its known zero combination whose weights are not all zero. Give each added vector weight 0. The old nonzero weights remain nonzero, and the extended sum is still zero.

FINAL ANSWER

Every subset of an independent collection is independent. Every superset of a dependent collection is dependent. The argument uses zero weights to pass between collections without changing the sum.

TRY IT YOURSELF · I4

FINAL ANSWER

The statement is false. Excluding the zero vector is necessary for independence, but is not sufficient: nonzero vectors may still repeat a direction.

7.1 Inputs, outputs, and reachable outputs

SEE THE IDEA

An image goes forward; a preimage solves backward

T(x) = Ax takes an input to an output. Finding an input for b means solving Ax = b.

  1. Input x in the domain
  2. Apply A
  3. Image Ax in the codomain
TaskMethod
Find T(x)Multiply
Find x with T(x) = bSolve [A | b]
Is b in the range?Test consistency

A function assigns exactly one output to every allowed input. A transformation or mapping is another name for a function. The domain lists allowed inputs. The codomain is the declared space containing the outputs. The image T(x) is the particular output produced by x. The range is the set of all outputs that are actually attained as x varies.

  1. For T: ℝ2ℝ^2 → ℝ3ℝ^3 with

    T(x)=AxT(x) = Ax

    and A a 3 × 2 matrix, each input has two entries and each output has three.

  2. The range is the span of A's columns, a subset of ℝ3ℝ^3.

  3. The codomain is still ℝ3ℝ^3 even if only a plane is attained.

  4. Do not shrink the codomain silently in order to make a statement about onto behavior true.

  1. Computing T(u) means multiplying A by a known input u.

  2. Finding an x with

    T(x)=bT(x) = b

    means solving

    Ax=bAx = b

  3. Checking whether b is in the range means deciding whether that system is consistent.

  4. These requests use different directions of the input-output relationship.

    0=10 = 1

  2. No choices of the unknowns can make that true.

  3. The system is inconsistent, and its solution set is empty.

  4. Free-looking coefficient columns cannot remove a contradiction.

  1. Thus b lies in the range and c does not.

  2. The columns are independent,

  3. so every reachable output has a unique input,

  4. but there are codomain vectors that are not reachable.

  5. This example anticipates the distinction between one-to-one and onto.

7.3 What linear means for a function

SEE THE IDEA

Linearity preserves weighted combinations

A linear map can move through addition and scalar multiplication.

T(cu+dv)=cT(u)+dT(v)T(cu + dv) = cT(u) + dT(v)
RuleLinear?Reason
T(x) = 2xYesPreserves every linear combination
T(x) = x + (1,0)NoT(0) ≠ 0
T(x) = x2x² in ℝNoT(2·1) ≠ 2T(1)

  1. Definition. T is linear if

    T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v)T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v)

    for every pair of domain vectors and T(cu) = cT(u) for every domain vector u and every real scalar c.

  2. The first property preserves addition;

  3. the second preserves scaling.

  4. Their combination gives T(cu + dv) = cT(u) + dT(v).

  5. This is the superposition principle: a weighted combination of inputs produces the same weighted combination of outputs.

Explore the Full Proof · Deeper Mathematical Explanation
  1. State the assumptions
  2. Use the definition
  3. Justify each implication
  4. Reach the claimed conclusion

  1. Every matrix transformation is linear because matrix-vector multiplication distributes over addition and scalar multiplication.

  2. For example,

    T(x1,x2)=(2x1−x2,3x2)T(x₁,x₂) = (2x₁ - x₂,3x₂)

    has matrix [2−103][2,-1;0,3].

  3. To prove the statement from the definition, let

    u=(u1,u2),v=(v1,v2)u = (u₁,u₂), v = (v₁,v₂)

  4. Then

    T(u+v)=(2u1+2v1−u2−v2,3u2+3v2)=T(u)+T(v)T(u + v) = (2u₁ + 2v₁ - u₂ - v₂,3u₂ + 3v₂) = T(u) + T(v)

  5. Also T(cu) = (2cu1u₁ - cu2u₂,3cu2u₂) = cT(u).

  6. Arbitrary letters make the proof cover all inputs.

  1. Every linear T sends zero to zero:

    T(0)=T(0u)=0T(u)=0T(0) = T(0u) = 0T(u) = 0

  2. This is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one.

  3. S(x1,x2)=(x1+1,x2)S(x₁,x₂) = (x₁ + 1,x₂)

    fails immediately because

    S(0)=(1,0)S(0) = (1,0)

  4. The rule

    Q(x1,x2)=(x12,x2)Q(x₁,x₂) = (x₁^2,x₂)

    passes the zero test but fails scaling:

    Q(2,0)=(4,0)Q(2,0) = (4,0)

    , while

    2Q(1,0)=(2,0)2Q(1,0) = (2,0)

  5. A counterexample proves failure;

  6. numerical examples of success cannot prove universal linearity.

7.4 Dilations, contractions, and shear

SEE THE IDEA

See what changes in a shear

Horizontal displacement depends on height; the second coordinate stays the same.

  1. The rule T(x) = rx scales every vector.

  2. For

    0≤r≤10 ≤ r ≤ 1

    it is a contraction in the lecture convention, including collapse at

    r=0r = 0

    and no change at

    r=1r = 1

  3. For r > 1 it is a dilation.

  4. A negative r also reverses direction.

  5. Multiplying by a scalar remains linear even when the picture shrinks or reverses.

  1. The lecture shear has

    A=[1301]A = [1,3;0,1]

  2. so

    T(x1,x2)=(x1+3x2,x2)T(x₁,x₂) = (x₁ + 3x₂,x₂)

  3. Points on the horizontal axis stay fixed.

  4. A point at height 2 moves 6 units horizontally, while its height is unchanged.

  5. The corners (0,0),(2,0),(2,2),(0,2) map to (0,0),(2,0),(8,2),(6,2), making a parallelogram.

  1. This figure uses shear factor 1 for a compact diagram: (x1x₁,x2x₂) becomes (x1x₁ + x2x₂,x2x₂).

  2. Every horizontal strip moves by an amount proportional to its height.

  3. A shear changes angles and lengths but still preserves vector addition and scalar multiplication.

  4. Linearity is about these algebraic properties, not preservation of every geometric measurement.

7.5 Using superposition without finding the entire matrix

SEE THE IDEA

Use known images as building blocks

If the input is already expressed as a combination, apply the same weights to the known images.

T(3u+2v)=3T(u)+2T(v)T(3u + 2v) = 3T(u) + 2T(v)

Remember. This shortcut requires the assumption that T is linear.

  1. Suppose

    T(u)=(2,1)T(u) = (2,1)

    and

    T(v)=(−1,3)T(v) = (-1,3)

    , as in Course Exercise 1.8.17.

  2. Then

    T(3u)=3(2,1)=(6,3),T(2v)=2(−1,3)=(−2,6)T(3u) = 3(2,1) = (6,3), T(2v) = 2(-1,3) = (-2,6)

    , and

    T(3u+2v)=(6,3)+(−2,6)=(4,9)T(3u + 2v) = (6,3) + (-2,6) = (4,9)

  3. The known input vectors may have different coordinates from their outputs;

  4. keep u and T(u) distinct.

  1. If a picture shows

    w=u+2vw = u + 2v

    , linearity gives

    T(w)=T(u)+2T(v)T(w) = T(u) + 2T(v)

  2. Draw the two output displacements head to tail.

  3. Do not assume the coordinates of w are unchanged unless the transformation is known to be the identity.

7.6 Practice

TRY IT YOURSELF · T1

T1. For T(x1x₁,x2x₂) = (x1x₁ + 2x2x₂, -x1x₁ + x2x₂), find T(3,-1), then find every input sent to (5,1).

Show Detailed Solution · T1

T1.

Compute the image of the given input

T(3,−1)=(3+2(−1),−3+(−1))T(3,-1) = (3 + 2(-1), -3 + (-1))
T(3,−1)=(3−2,−3−1)=(1,−4)T(3,-1) = (3-2,-3-1) = (1,-4)

A preimage is an input giving the requested output

x1+2x2=5x_1 + 2x_2 = 5
−x1+x2=1-x_1 + x_2 = 1

Add the equations to eliminate x1x₁

3x2=63x_2 = 6
x2=2x_2 = 2
x1=5−2(2)=1x_1 = 5 - 2(2) = 1

Verify the preimage and its uniqueness

T(1,2)=(1+4,−1+2)=(5,1)T(1,2) = (1 + 4,-1 + 2) = (5,1)

Each input coordinate is fixed by the equations; neither is free. Equivalently, both coefficient columns have pivots.

FINAL ANSWER

The image of (3,−1) is (1,−4). The unique input for output (5,1) is (1,2).

TRY IT YOURSELF · T2

T2. Decide whether S(x1x₁,x2x₂) = (x1x₁,x2x₂ + 3) and Q(x1x₁,x2x₂) = (x1x₁x2x₂,0) are linear. Give precise reasons.

Show Detailed Solution · T2

T2.

Test S at zero

S(0,0)=(0,3)S(0,0) = (0,3)

A linear map must send the zero input to the zero output. This nonzero output already disproves linearity of S.

Passing the zero test is not enough for Q

Q(0,0)=(0,0)Q(0,0) = (0,0)

We must also test whether addition is preserved.

Compare the two sides of additivity

Q((1,0)+(0,1))=Q(1,1)=(1,0)Q((1,0)+(0,1)) = Q(1,1) = (1,0)
Q(1,0)+Q(0,1)=(0,0)+(0,0)=(0,0)Q(1,0) + Q(0,1) = (0,0) + (0,0) = (0,0)

The two outputs differ. One valid failure is enough to disprove a property required for all inputs.

FINAL ANSWER

Neither S nor Q is linear. S fails the zero test; Q fails the addition test.

TRY IT YOURSELF · T3

T3. If T(u) = (1,2), T(v) = (3,-1), find T(2u - v), explaining the assumption needed.

Show Detailed Solution · T3

T3.

Use the given linearity assumption

T(2u−v)=2T(u)−T(v)T(2u-v) = 2T(u) - T(v)

Linearity allows the same input weights to be used on the output vectors.

Scale the first known image

2[12]=[24]2[1;2] = [2;4]

Subtract the other image coordinate by coordinate

[24]−[3−1]=[2−34−(−1)]=[−15][2;4] - [3;-1] = [2-3;4-(-1)] = [-1;5]
FINAL ANSWER
T(2u−v)=[−15]T(2u-v) = [-1;5]

Without linearity, knowing only T(u) and T(v) would not determine this image.

chapters.html:
Source correspondence: Combined PDF pages 71-79; exercise PDF page 12.

8.1 Standard basis vectors isolate one coordinate

SEE THE IDEA

Standard basis vectors turn on one input at a time

Because eje_j has a single 1, multiplying by it selects column j.

A=[T(e1)T(e2)]A = [T(e_1),T(e_2)]

  1. The standard basis vector eje_j has a 1 in coordinate j and 0 in every other coordinate.

  2. In

    ℝ3,e1=(1,0,0),e2=(0,1,0),e3=(0,0,1)ℝ^3, e₁ = (1,0,0), e₂ = (0,1,0), e₃ = (0,0,1)

  3. Every

    x=(x1,x2,x3)x = (x₁,x₂,x₃)

    equals x1x₁e1e₁ + x2x₂e2e₂ + x3x₃e3e₃.

  4. This is a coordinate identity: the coefficients simply reconstruct the entries.

  1. If T is linear,

    T(x)=x1T(e1)+T(x) = x₁T(e₁) +

    ... + xnx_nT(ene_n).

  2. Therefore the standard matrix is A = [T(e1e₁) ...

  3. T(ene_n)].

  4. The output vectors become columns, not rows, because Ax combines columns with input weights.

  5. A has m rows when each T(eje_j) has m entries, and n columns when there are n input coordinates.

  1. Theorem (supplied Theorem 10). Every linear transformation ℝnℝ^n → ℝmℝ^m has a unique such matrix.

  2. Existence follows from the expansion just given.

  3. For uniqueness, if B also represents T, then its jth column is Be

    _j=T(ej)_j = T(e_j)

  4. so every column of B equals the corresponding column of A.

  5. Thus

    B=AB = A

  6. This is a proof for arbitrary dimensions, not a pattern guessed from one example.

8.2 Reading the matrix from a rule

SEE THE IDEA

Read coefficients by output row

Each output coordinate becomes one row of the standard matrix.

T(x1,x2)=(x1−3x2,−2x1+x2,x1)T(x_1,x_2) = (x_1 - 3x_2, -2x_1 + x_2, x_1)

  1. For

    T(x1,x2)=(x1−3x2,−2x1+x2,x1)T(x₁,x₂) = (x₁ - 3x₂,-2x₁ + x₂,x₁)

    , substituting

    e1=(1,0)e₁ = (1,0)

    gives (1,-2,1), and

    e2=(0,1)e₂ = (0,1)

    gives (-3,1,0).

  2. Hence:

[1−3−2110]

  1. The first row computes x1x₁ - 3x2x₂, the second computes -2x1x₁ + x2x₂, and the third computes x1x₁.

  2. A zero coefficient is an actual matrix entry;

  3. do not omit the 0 at the lower right.

  4. You may read coefficients directly once you understand why the column construction works.

8.3 Transformation reference with geometric meaning

SEE THE IDEA

A familiar picture has a precise rule

A reflection changes a sign; a projection deletes a coordinate.

Horizontal reflection

Horizontal projection

  1. The following matrices reproduce the types in the supplied geometric tables.

  2. Each is 2 × 2 and acts on a column (x1x₁,x2x₂).

  3. You can recover every matrix by applying the rule to e1e₁ and e2e₂.

  1. Reflection in the horizontal axis:

    (x1,x2)↦(x1,−x2)(x₁,x₂) ↦ (x₁,-x₂)

    , matrix [100−1][1,0;0,-1]. Reflection in the vertical axis:

    (x1,x2)↦(−x1,x2)(x₁,x₂) ↦ (-x₁,x₂)

    , matrix [−1001][-1,0;0,1]. **Reflection in

    x2=x1x₂ = x₁

    : swap coordinates, matrix [0110][0,1;1,0]. Reflection in

    x2=−x1x₂ = -x₁

    : swap and negate, matrix [0−1−10][0,-1;-1,0]. Reflection in the origin:** negate both coordinates, matrix [−100−1][-1,0;0,-1].

  1. Horizontal scale by k: (kx1x₁,x2x₂), matrix [k001][k,0;0,1]. Vertical scale by k: (x1x₁,kx2x₂), matrix [100k][1,0;0,k].

  2. For the positive-scale tables, 0 < k < 1 contracts the named direction and k > 1 stretches it.

  3. Scaling both directions by k uses kI2I₂.

  1. Horizontal shear by k: (x1x₁ + kx2x₂,x2x₂), matrix [1k01][1,k;0,1]. Vertical shear by k: (x1x₁,kx1x₁ + x2x₂), matrix [10k1][1,0;k,1].

  2. The sign of k chooses the direction of the slant.

  1. Projection onto the horizontal axis: (x1x₁,0), matrix [1000][1,0;0,0]. Projection onto the vertical axis: (0,x2x₂), matrix [0001][0,0;0,1].

  2. A projection discards a coordinate and cannot later recover it uniquely.

  1. The supplied exercises also require rotations.

  2. For counterclockwise angle θ, the standard matrix is [cos θ−sin θsin θcos θ][cos θ,-sin θ;sin θ,cos θ].

  3. The first column is the rotated unit vector (cos θ,sin θ);

  4. the second is its perpendicular companion (-sin θ,cos θ).

  5. A clockwise rotation uses negative θ.

  6. For

    θ=π2θ = π/2

    the columns are (0,1) and (-1,0);

  7. for

    θ=πθ = π

    they are (-1,0) and (0,-1).

  8. Angles in the course exercises are in radians: π radians is a half-turn, π/2 a quarter-turn, and 2π a full turn.

  9. The values at π/4 use

    cos (π4)=sin (π4)=12cos(π/4) = sin(π/4) = 1/√2

8.4 Composing geometric actions

SEE THE IDEA

The rightmost matrix acts first

Keep the action order visible before multiplying.

  1. Input x
  2. First S: A_S x
  3. Then T: A_T(A_S x)
  4. Combined matrix A_T A_S

  1. When a rule says 'first S, then T,' apply S to e1e₁ and then T to that result;

  2. repeat with e2e₂.

  3. Put the two final outputs into columns.

  4. After matrix multiplication is introduced, the same process has matrix A_T A_S.

  5. The action performed first is the rightmost factor.

  1. For the supplied Exercise 1.9.8, first reflect in the horizontal axis and then in

    x2=x1x₂ = x₁

  2. The first reflection sends (x1x₁,x2x₂) to (x1x₁,-x2x₂);

  3. the second swaps entries, giving (-x2x₂,x1x₁).

  4. Thus e1e₁ becomes e2e₂ and e2e₂ becomes -e1e₁.

  5. The matrix [0−110][0,-1;1,0] is a counterclockwise quarter-turn.

  6. Reversing the order produces a different rotation.

8.5 Onto asks about existence for every codomain vector

SEE THE IDEA

Onto asks whether every output is reachable

There must be a pivot in every output row of the coefficient matrix.

  1. A mapping T: ℝnℝ^n → ℝmℝ^m is onto ℝmℝ^m if every b in that declared codomain equals T(x) for at least one input x.

  2. In matrix language,

    Ax=bAx = b

    is consistent for every

    b∈ℝmb ∈ ℝ^m

  3. This is equivalent to the columns spanning ℝmℝ^m and to a pivot in every row of A.

  1. Being able to find an input for one specific b is insufficient.

  2. The map

    T(x1,x2)=(x1,0)T(x₁,x₂) = (x₁,0)

    produces (3,0) but cannot produce (0,1),

  3. so it is not onto ℝ2ℝ^2.

  4. It would be onto the horizontal axis if that were the declared codomain,

  5. but that is a different mapping specification.

8.6 One-to-one asks about collisions of inputs

SEE THE IDEA

One-to-one asks whether inputs collide

If a nonzero input produces zero, it collides with the zero input.

  1. Au = Av
  2. A(u − v) = 0
  3. Only zero solves Az = 0?
  4. Then u − v = 0, so u = v

  1. A mapping is one-to-one when different inputs cannot produce the same output.

  2. Equivalently, each codomain vector has at most one preimage.

  3. Unreachable outputs are allowed in this definition.

  4. For a linear mapping, one-to-one is equivalent to

    Ax=0Ax = 0

    having only the trivial solution, to independent columns, and to a pivot in every column of A.

Explore the Full Proof · Deeper Mathematical Explanation
  1. State the assumptions
  2. Use the definition
  3. Justify each implication
  4. Reach the claimed conclusion

  1. Here is the proof linking collisions to the homogeneous test.

  2. If

    Au=AvAu = Av

    , then

    A(u−v)=0A(u - v) = 0

  3. If only zero goes to zero,

    u−v=0u - v = 0

    and therefore

    u=vu = v

  4. Conversely, if a nonzero z satisfies

    Az=0Az = 0

    , then z and 0 are different inputs with the same output.

  5. So the mapping fails to be one-to-one.

  1. The diagram shows projection.

  2. Two distinct inputs with the same first coordinate collide, and outputs with nonzero second coordinate are missed.

  3. Projection is neither one-to-one nor onto ℝ2ℝ^2.

  4. It supplies a visible reason for both failures, which are logically separate.

8.7 Compare all four possibilities

SEE THE IDEA

Existence and uniqueness are different axes

Square and invertible gives both; rectangular maps can have just one.

MapOnto?One-to-one?
(x,y) ↦ (x,y)Yes, into ℝ2ℝ²Yes
(x,y) ↦ xYes, into ℝNo
x ↦ (x,0)No, into ℝ2ℝ²Yes
(x,y) ↦ (x,0)No, into ℝ2ℝ²No

  1. The inclusion T:

    ℝ2→ℝ3,T(a,b)=(a,b,0)ℝ^2 → ℝ^3, T(a,b) = (a,b,0)

    , has a pivot in each of its two columns.

  2. It is one-to-one because the input can be read back from the first two output entries.

  3. It is not onto ℝ3ℝ^3 because outputs with nonzero third entry are impossible.

  1. The map T:

    ℝ3→ℝ2,T(a,b,c)=(a,b)ℝ^3 → ℝ^2, T(a,b,c) = (a,b)

    , has a pivot in each of its two rows.

  2. It is onto because every (a,b) is attained,

  3. but not one-to-one because c can vary freely.

  4. An invertible 2 × 2 scaling with nonzero factors is both.

  5. The zero map ℝ2ℝ^2 → ℝ2ℝ^2 is neither.

  1. For an m × n matrix, onto requires m pivots and therefore

    n≥mn ≥ m

  2. One-to-one requires n pivots and therefore

    m≥nm ≥ n

  3. For a square matrix these conditions coincide.

  4. For rectangular matrices they need not.

  5. The lecture's 3 × 4 echelon example [1−48102−130005][1,-4,8,1;0,2,-1,3;0,0,0,5] is onto ℝ3ℝ^3 but not one-to-one: it has three row pivots and one nonpivot input column.

8.8 Practice

TRY IT YOURSELF · M1

M1. Find the standard matrix for T(a,b) = (2a + b,a - b,3b). Decide whether it is one-to-one and onto its declared codomain ℝ3ℝ^3.

Show Detailed Solution · M1

M1.

Put the two basis images in columns

T(e1)=[210]T(e_1) = [2;1;0]
T(e2)=[1−13]T(e_2) = [1;-1;3]

Test one-to-one behavior with zero output

Ax=0A x = 0
3x2=03x_2 = 0
x2=0x_2 = 0
2x1+0=02x_1 + 0 = 0
x1=0x_1 = 0

Only the zero input produces zero. Therefore different inputs cannot collide: if Au = Av, then A(u − v) = 0 forces u = v.

Test onto behavior separately

Two columns can supply at most two pivots. Three output rows would require three pivots for onto ℝ3ℝ³.

Exhibit an unreachable output

Ax=[001]A x = [0;0;1]
3x2=13x_2 = 1
x2=13x_2 = 1/3
x1−x2=0x_1 - x_2 = 0
x1=13x_1 = 1/3
2(13)+13=12(1/3) + 1/3 = 1

The first requested output is 0, but these forced input values produce 1. The target is unreachable.

FINAL ANSWER

The standard matrix is the displayed 3 × 2 matrix. The map is one-to-one and is not onto ℝ3ℝ³.

TRY IT YOURSELF · M2

M2. Find the matrix for first reflecting in the vertical axis and then projecting onto the horizontal axis. Explain both lost information and attainable outputs.

Show Detailed Solution · M2

M2.

Apply the reflection first

(a,b)↦(−a,b)(a,b) ↦ (-a,b)

Apply the horizontal projection second

(−a,b)↦(−a,0)(-a,b) ↦ (-a,0)
[−1000]

Inspect the possible outputs

Every output has second coordinate 0, so (0,1) can never occur. Every horizontal output (c,0) occurs by choosing a = −c. Thus the range is exactly the horizontal axis.

Find distinct inputs with the same output

(1,0)↦(−1,0)(1,0) ↦ (-1,0)
(1,2)↦(−1,0)(1,2) ↦ (-1,0)

The second input coordinate is erased. These distinct inputs collide.

FINAL ANSWER

The map is neither onto ℝ2ℝ² nor one-to-one. Its standard matrix is the displayed diagonal matrix.

TRY IT YOURSELF · M3

M3. Give a matrix mapping ℝ3ℝ^3 onto ℝ2ℝ^2 that is not one-to-one, and a matrix mapping ℝ2ℝ^2 one-to-one into ℝ3ℝ^3 that is not onto. Justify by pivots.

Show Detailed Solution · M3

M3.

Onto does not force one-to-one

[100010]
(a,b,c)↦(a,b)(a,b,c) ↦ (a,b)

Every two-entry output is reached, but c can be anything. There is a pivot in each row and a free third input.

One-to-one does not force onto

[100100]
(a,b)↦(a,b,0)(a,b) ↦ (a,b,0)

The output uniquely records both inputs. But any three-entry target with nonzero last coordinate is missed. There is a pivot in each column and no pivot in row 3.

FINAL ANSWER

The first matrix is onto ℝ2ℝ² and not one-to-one. The second is one-to-one into ℝ3ℝ³ and not onto ℝ3ℝ³.

chapters.html:
Source correspondence: Combined PDF pages 80-90; exercise PDF pages 13-14.

9.1 Entries, equality, and entrywise operations

SEE THE IDEA

Rows first, columns second

A matrix entry aijaᵢⱼ is in row i and column j. Entrywise operations require the same shape.

2[1234]+[0110]=[2578]2[1,2;3,4] + [0,1;1,0] = [2,5;7,8]

  1. If A is m × n, aija_{ij} is its entry in row i, column j.

  2. The column aja_j consists of a1ja_{1j},...,amja_{mj}.

  3. A diagonal entry has matching indices.

  4. A diagonal matrix is square and has zero entries off its main diagonal.

  5. An identity matrix is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are all 1.

  6. A zero matrix can be any size;

  7. all its entries are zero.

  1. Matrices are equal only if their dimensions match and every corresponding entry agrees.

  2. Addition and subtraction require equal dimensions and operate entrywise.

  3. Multiplying by a scalar scales every entry.

  4. For

    A=[1−234]A = [1,-2;3,4]

    and

    B=[25−10],A+B=[3324],A−B=[−1−744]B = [2,5;-1,0], A + B = [3,3;2,4], A - B = [-1,-7;4,4]

    , and

    −2A=[−24−6−8]-2A = [-2,4;-6,-8]

  5. These operations retain the original dimensions.

  1. Addition is commutative and associative.

  2. A+0=AA + 0 = A

  3. Scalars distribute over a sum of matrices and a sum of scalars: r(A + B) = rA + rB and (r + s)A = rA + sA.

  4. Also r(sA) = (rs)A.

  5. Matching dimensions are part of every statement.

  6. A 2 × 3 matrix cannot be added to a 3 × 2 matrix just because both contain six entries.

9.2 Why matrix multiplication is defined differently

SEE THE IDEA

One row and one column make one entry

Matrix multiplication composes weighted sums; it is not entrywise multiplication.

Choose one row

Choose one column

c11=(2)(4)+(3)(1)=11c_{11} = (2)(4) + (3)(1) = 11
  1. Pair corresponding entries
  2. Multiply each pair
  3. Add to get one output entry

  1. Suppose B transforms x into Bx, then A transforms that output into A(Bx).

  2. We want one matrix C that has the same effect.

  3. Each column bjb_j of B is the image of eje_j after the first transformation,

  4. so the final image is Abjb_j.

  5. Therefore

    C=ABC = AB

    has columns Ab1b₁,...,Abpb_p.

  1. If A is m × n and B is n × p, then AB is m × p.

  2. The matching n is the number of entries in each column of B, which A must be able to multiply.

  3. The output has m entries for each of the p input coordinate directions.

  4. Thus the mnemonic 'inside sizes agree, outside sizes give the answer' has a mathematical reason.

  1. The entry formula is

    (AB)ij=ai1b1j+(AB)_{ij} = a_{i1}b_{1j} +

    ... + ain a_{in}bnjb_{nj}.

  2. It multiplies a row by a column, not matching entries in place.

  3. Entrywise multiplication is a different operation and is not what AB denotes here.

9.3 Full lecture product: square times rectangular

SEE THE IDEA

Place each computed entry in its own location

The source example calculates a 2 × 3 output, six entries in all.

Choose one row

Choose one column

c11=(2)(4)+(3)(1)=11c_{11} = (2)(4) + (3)(1) = 11
  1. Pair corresponding entries
  2. Multiply each pair
  3. Add to get one output entry

Remember. Compute c11c₁₁ first, then use the same rule for each remaining row–column pair.

  1. Combined PDF pages 85-86 use

    A=[231−5]A = [2,3;1,-5]

    and

    B=[4361−23]B = [4,3,6;1,-2,3]

  2. A is 2 × 2, B is 2 × 3,

  3. so AB is 2 × 3.

  4. There are six entries to compute, and all six are shown.

In this calculation, A is the left factor and B is the right factor.

Read A: 2 rows, 2 columns

A row runs horizontally, from left to right. A column runs vertically, from top to bottom. Count rows first when writing a size.

Read B: 2 rows, 3 columns

Check that multiplication is allowed

(2 × 2)(2 × 3)→ 2 × 3

The highlighted inner counts are both 2: every row of the left factor has one entry for every row of the right factor. The outside counts tell us the output has 2 rows and 3 columns.

Calculate output row 1, column 1

Take row 1 of A and column 1 of B. Pair entries in their original order: multiply the first pair, the second pair, and so on. Then add.

c11=(2)(4)+(3)(1)=11c_{11} = (2)(4) + (3)(1) = 11
8+38 + 3

c12=(2)(3)+(3)(−2)=0c_{12} = (2)(3) + (3)(-2) = 0
6−66 - 6
00

Take row 1 of A and column 3 of B. Pair entries in their original order: multiply the first pair, the second pair, and so on. Then add.

Put the entries into their output positions

Check the result one output column at a time

For each output column, use the matching column of the right factor as weights on all columns of the left factor. This is the same row arithmetic grouped vertically.

c1=(4)[21]+(1)[3−5]=[11−1]c_1 = (4)[2;1] + (1)[3;-5] = [11;-1]
c2=(3)[21]+(−2)[3−5]=[013]c_2 = (3)[2;1] + (-2)[3;-5] = [0;13]

FINAL ANSWER

Dimensions: (2 × 2)(2 × 3) = 2 × 3.

  1. The other order BA is undefined here: B has three columns and A has two rows.

  2. Noncommutativity can therefore mean that one order is not even meaningful.

  3. For square matrices both orders exist,

  4. but their entries can still differ.

9.4 Associativity does not permit reordering

SEE THE IDEA

Regrouping is different from reordering

Associativity moves parentheses. It does not move factors past each other.

(AB)C=A(BC)(AB)C = A(BC)
AB=BAAB = BA

The second equation is generally false.

  1. For compatible sizes,

    (AB)C=A(BC)(AB)C = A(BC)

  2. This allows regrouping, not exchanging A and B.

  3. Acting on a vector, both sides perform C first, then B, then A.

  4. The column definition also proves the identity: the jth column of (AB)C is (AB)cjc_j = A(Bcjc_j), the jth column of A(BC).

  1. The distributive laws are

    A(B+C)=AB+ACA(B + C) = AB + AC

    and

    (B+C)A=BA+CA(B + C)A = BA + CA

  2. A scalar may be factored consistently: r(AB) = (rA

    )B=A())B = A(

    rB).

  3. Identity matrices have the appropriate side sizes:

    ImA=AI_m A = A

    and

    AIn=AA I_n = A

    when A is m × n.

  1. For

    A=[1101]A = [1,1;0,1]

    and

    B=[1002],AB=[1202]B = [1,0;0,2], AB = [1,2;0,2]

    whereas

    BA=[1102]BA = [1,1;0,2]

  2. Applying B first doubles vertical coordinates before the shear mixes them horizontally;

  3. reversing the order changes the result.

  4. Hence

    AB=BAAB = BA

    is a special property, called commuting, not a general multiplication law.

9.5 Zero products and failed cancellation

SEE THE IDEA

A matrix may erase information

A zero product does not force a zero factor.

AB=[0000]AB = [0,0;0,0]

Remember. An invertible factor is needed for cancellation.

  1. Nonzero matrices can multiply to zero.

  2. Let

    A=[1000]A = [1,0;0,0]

    and

    B=[0001]B = [0,0;0,1]

  3. Both are nonzero,

  4. but

    AB=0AB = 0

    because A removes the output direction produced by B.

  5. Therefore

    AB=0AB = 0

    does not imply

    A=0A = 0

    or

    B=0B = 0

  1. For the same A, take

    C=0C = 0

  2. Then

    AB=ACAB = AC

    even though

    B≠CB ≠ C

  3. You cannot cancel A without an appropriate invertibility assumption.

  4. Matrix 'division' is not an operation that can be used without checking such assumptions.

  5. Similarly, (A + B)^2 expands to A2A^2 + AB + BA + B2B^2;

  6. it becomes A2A^2 + 2AB + B2B^2 only if A and B commute.

9.6 Powers and repeated transformations

SEE THE IDEA

A power repeats the same action

For a square A, A2A²x applies A twice to x.

  1. x
  2. Ax
  3. A(Ax) = A2A²x

Remember. A0A⁰ = I. Negative powers require an inverse.

  1. For square A and positive integer k, AkA^k means k copies multiplied in order.

  2. It does not raise each entry to the kth power.

  3. For

    A=[1101],A2=[1201]A = [1,1;0,1], A^2 = [1,2;0,1]

    because two horizontal shears add their effects.

  4. Its top right entry is 2, even though

    12=11^2 = 1

  5. By convention

    A0=IA^0 = I

    of the matching size.

  6. Powers with negative exponents require invertibility and are discussed through inverses.

9.7 Transpose switches rows and columns

SEE THE IDEA

Transpose swaps the two indices

Turn each row into the corresponding column.

(AB)T=BTAT(AB)^T = B^T A^T

  1. For an m × n matrix A, ATA^T is n × m and has

    (AT)ij=aji(A^T)_{ij} = a_{ji}

  2. For

    A=[123456]A = [1,2,3;4,5,6]

    , the transpose is [142536][1,4;2,5;3,6].

  3. A transpose is not an inverse: it changes the arrangement and size, not necessarily the effect of a transformation in reverse.

  1. The supplied transpose identities are (ATA^T)^T = A, (A + B)^T = ATA^T + BTB^T, (rA)^T = rATA^T, and

    (AB)T=BTAT(AB)^T = B^T A^T

  2. The product order reverses.

  3. If A is m × n and B is n × p, (AB)^T is p × m.

  4. The product BTB^T ATA^T has size (p × n)(n × m), which matches;

  5. ATA^T BTB^T often fails even the size test.

  1. A proof of the last identity examines entry i,j.

  2. Entry i,j of (AB)^T is entry j,i of AB, namely Σ over k of ajka_{jk}bkib_{ki}.

  3. Entry i,j of BTB^T ATA^T is Σ over k of

    (BT)ik(AT)kj=Σ(B^T)_{ik}(A^T)_{kj} = Σ

    over k of bkib_{ki}ajka_{jk}, the same real-number sum.

  4. Equal dimensions and entrywise equality prove the identity.

chapters.title: 10. Section 2.2 - The inverse of a matrix
chapters.html:
Source correspondence: Combined PDF pages 91-100; exercise PDF pages 15-16.

10.1 Undoing a transformation

SEE THE IDEA

Undo the change in the opposite direction

A shear changes the first coordinate by adding the second; its inverse subtracts it.

  1. (x1x₁,x2x₂)
  2. A: (x1x₁+x2x₂,x2x₂)
  3. A−1A⁻¹: ((x1x₁+x2x₂)−x2x₂,x2x₂)
  4. Original (x1x₁,x2x₂) restored

  1. An inverse reverses the effect of a square matrix on every input.

  2. An n × n matrix A is invertible if an n × n matrix C satisfies both

    AC=InAC = I_n

    and

    CA=InCA = I_n

  3. This C is A−1A^(-1).

  4. A noninvertible square matrix is singular;

  5. an invertible one is nonsingular.

  6. In this course definition, an ordinary two-sided inverse is only defined for square matrices.

  1. The notation A−1A^(-1) is not formed by taking reciprocals of entries.

  2. The identity conditions involve matrix multiplication.

  3. A projection is singular because it sends many different inputs to the same output;

  4. no inverse can know which original input to restore.

  5. A nonzero uniform scaling is invertible: scaling by r is undone by scaling by 1/r.

  1. If B and C are both inverses of

    A,B=BI=B(AC)=(BA)C=IC=CA, B = BI = B(AC) = (BA)C = IC = C

  2. Thus the inverse, when it exists, is unique.

  3. Each equality has a reason: identity, inverse condition, associativity, inverse condition, identity.

  4. This short chain is a model university proof.

  1. The figure shears by (x1x₁ + x2x₂,x2x₂).

  2. Given the output y, subtract y2y₂ from y1y₁ to recover the input: (y1y₁ - y2y₂,y2y₂).

  3. The forward matrix [1101][1,1;0,1] and backward matrix [1−101][1,-1;0,1] multiply in either order to I2I₂.

10.2 Deriving the 2 × 2 formula

SEE THE IDEA

Check the denominator before dividing

The determinant ad − bc tells whether this two-dimensional map can be undone.

A−1=(1ad−bc)[d−b−ca]A^(-1) = (1/(ad-bc))[d,-b;-c,a]
ConditionMeaning
ad − bc ≠ 0The formula is defined; A is invertible.
ad − bc = 0No two-sided inverse exists.

  1. Let

    A=[abcd]A = [a,b;c,d]

  2. Seek a matrix that removes the off-diagonal effects.

  3. Try

    C=[d−b−ca]C = [d,-b;-c,a]

  4. Multiplying gives AC = [ad - bc, -ab + ba;

  5. cd - dc, -cb + da] = (ad - bc)I2I₂.

  6. Multiplying in the reverse order also gives (ad - bc)I2I₂.

  7. If

    δ=ad−bcδ = ad - bc

    is nonzero, divide C by δ to obtain the inverse.

A−1=(1ad−bc)[d−b−ca],provided ad−bc≠0.A^(-1) = (1/(ad - bc)) [d,-b; -c,a], provided ad - bc ≠ 0.

  1. Here a,b,c,d are the four entries of A.

  2. The scalar ad - bc is its 2 × 2 determinant.

  3. The formula swaps the two diagonal entries, negates the two off-diagonal entries, and divides every resulting entry by the determinant.

  4. The order of ad and bc matters.

  5. The condition is

    ad−bc≠0ad - bc ≠ 0

    , not

    ab−cd≠0ab - cd ≠ 0

  1. Why is A singular when

    ad−bc=0ad - bc = 0

    ?

  2. If the first row is nonzero,

    z=(−b,a)z = (-b,a)

    is a nonzero vector and

    Az=(0,ad−bc)=0Az = (0,ad - bc) = 0

  3. An inverse would imply

    z=A−10=0z = A^(-1)0 = 0

    , a contradiction.

  4. If the first row is zero and the second is nonzero, use

    z=(−d,c)z = (-d,c)

  5. If both rows are zero, every nonzero vector is sent to zero.

  6. These cases establish the determinant condition without dividing by a possibly zero entry.

10.3 Numerical examples and direct verification

SEE THE IDEA

Verify with multiplication, not resemblance

SEE THE IDEA

Multiply by the undo operation

When A is invertible, left-multiplication isolates the input.

  1. Ax = b
  2. A−1A⁻¹Ax = A−1A⁻¹b
  3. Ix = A−1A⁻¹b
  4. x = A−1A⁻¹b

    Ax=bAx = b

    by A−1A^(-1):

    A(A−1b)=bA(A^(-1)b) = b
