10.5 Elementary matrices turn row operations into products

SEE THE IDEA

An elementary matrix performs one row operation

Apply the row operation to I to get E; left-multiplication EA performs it on A.

  1. Row 1 of EA = row 1 of A
  2. Row 2 of EA = row 2 of A − 3 row 1 of A

  1. An elementary matrix is obtained from I by performing exactly one elementary row operation.

  2. Left-multiplying a compatible A by E performs that same operation on A.

  3. For example,

    E=[100010−401]E = [1,0,0;0,1,0;-4,0,1]

    replaces row 3 of A by row 3 minus four times row 1.

  4. This follows directly from the row-column multiplication rule: the third output row combines input rows with weights -4,0,1.

  1. Swapping rows 1 and 2 of I3I₃ gives [010100001][0,1,0;1,0,0;0,0,1].

  2. Scaling row 3 by 5 gives [100010005][1,0,0;0,1,0;0,0,5].

  3. Each elementary matrix is invertible because its row operation is reversible.

  4. Their inverses respectively add four times row 1 to row 3, swap the same rows again, and scale row 3 by 151/5.

  5. Right multiplication would act on columns and is not the row-operation model used in this theorem.

10.6 Why augmenting with I finds the inverse

SEE THE IDEA

Carry the identity through the same operations

The row operations that turn A into I simultaneously turn I into A−1A⁻¹.

  1. [A | I]
  2. Apply every operation to both blocks
  3. [I | A−1A⁻¹]

Remember. The right block is the answer only when the left block is exactly I.

  1. Theorem (supplied Theorem 7). A square matrix A is invertible exactly when it is row equivalent to I.

  2. A sequence of row operations that reduces A to I transforms I into A−1A^(-1).

  1. If the row operations correspond to E1E₁,...,EpE_p, their total effect is EpE_p ...

  2. E1A=IE₁ A = I

  3. Write

    E=EpE = E_p

    ...

  4. E1E₁.

  5. Since all elementary matrices are invertible, E is invertible and

    A=E−1A = E^(-1)

  6. so

    E=A−1E = A^(-1)

  7. Applying the same operations to I gives

    EI=E=A−1EI = E = A^(-1)

  8. Therefore [A | I] reduces to [I | A−1A^(-1)].

  9. The augmented columns are carried along exactly as right-hand sides were in solving systems.

  1. If A is invertible,

    Ax=bAx = b

    is solvable for every b,

  2. so A has a pivot in every row.

  3. Since it is square, there is also a pivot in every column, and

    RREF(A)=IRREF(A) = I

  4. This proves the other direction and connects inversion with the earlier pivot criteria.

10.8 Recognizing failure and finding selected columns

One inverse column needs only one target

Column j of A−1A⁻¹ is the input that maps to eje_j.

Ax=ejA x = e_j

  3. Read x as inverse column j

10.9 Inverse identities and why order reverses

SEE THE IDEA

Undo the last action first

If AB applies B and then A, its inverse must undo A and then B.

  1. x → Bx → ABx
  2. Undo A with A−1A⁻¹
  3. Undo B with B−1B⁻¹
(AB)−1=B−1A−1(AB)^(-1) = B^(-1)A^(-1)

  1. For invertible square matrices of matching size,

    (A−1)−1=A,(AB)−1=B−1A−1(A^(-1))^(-1) = A, (AB)^(-1) = B^(-1)A^(-1)

    , and

    (AT)−1=(A−1)T(A^T)^(-1) = (A^(-1))^T

  2. For the product identity,

    (AB)(B−1A−1)=A(BB−1)A−1=I(AB)(B^(-1)A^(-1)) = A(BB^(-1))A^(-1) = I

    , and the reverse product is also I.

  3. You undo the last action first, just as a shear followed by a stretch is undone by undoing the stretch and then the shear.

  1. For the transpose identity, transpose

    AA−1=IAA^(-1) = I

    to get

    (A−1)TAT=I(A^(-1))^T A^T = I

  2. Transpose the other inverse equation to get

    AT(A−1)T=IA^T(A^(-1))^T = I

  3. Thus both defining equations hold.

  4. There is no general identity

    (A+B)−1=A−1+B−1(A + B)^(-1) = A^(-1) + B^(-1)

  5. even 1 × 1 matrices give a counterexample:

    (1+1)−1=12(1 + 1)^(-1) = 1/2

  6. whereas

    1−1+1−1=21^(-1) + 1^(-1) = 2

chapters.title: 11. Writing proofs and solving unfamiliar questions
chapters.html:
11.1 Translate the request before calculating

SEE THE IDEA

Translate the request into a test

Start by identifying the mathematical object and the actual goal.

Question asksTranslate into
Is b in the span?Do weights exist: Ax = b?
Independent?Are zero weights the only solution of Ac = 0?
Onto?Is every coefficient row a pivot row?
Invertible?Can a square A reduce to I?

  1. 'Is b in a span?' asks for existence of weights,

  2. so build [A | b]. 'Are these vectors independent?' asks whether

    Ax=0Ax = 0

    has only zero as a solution. 'Does T map onto its codomain?' asks for a row pivot for every output coordinate. 'Is T one-to-one?' asks for a column pivot for every input coordinate. 'Find the standard matrix' asks for T(eje_j) as columns. 'Find an inverse' asks for [A | I] to become [I | C], then verification.

  1. A question can ask for several of these at once.

  2. For example, if A is 3 × 4 with three pivots, it is onto ℝ3ℝ^3 and its columns span ℝ3ℝ^3.

  3. It is not one-to-one and its columns are dependent.

  4. Every b has infinitely many solutions because every b is consistent and there is one free input variable.

  5. A single pivot count supports all these statements,

  6. but each needs its own interpretation.

11.2 A practical proof pattern

SEE THE IDEA

Build an argument, one justified link at a time

Each theorem has assumptions; check them before using its conclusion.

  1. Assumptions
  2. Definition of the target
  3. A justified deduction
  4. Conclusion in the question’s language
Explore the Full Proof · Deeper Mathematical Explanation
  1. State the assumptions
  2. Use the definition
  3. Justify each implication
  4. Reach the claimed conclusion

  1. First state the assumptions.

  2. Next state the target in the relevant definition.

  3. Then use a theorem whose assumptions are satisfied.

  4. Finally connect the result back to the target.

  5. For instance, to prove that adding a vector in a span does not change the span, suppose

    w=c1v1+w = c₁v₁ +

    ... + cpc_pvpv_p.

  6. Every combination of the original vectors remains available after w is added, proving one inclusion.

  7. Conversely, a combination of the enlarged collection can replace its w term by that expression, producing a combination of the original vectors.

  8. Both inclusions prove equality of the spans.

  1. A counterexample must satisfy all stated assumptions.

  2. To disprove 'a consistent system has a unique solution,' use

    x1+x2=1x₁ + x₂ = 1

  3. It is consistent because (1,0) works,

  4. but (0,1) is a different solution.

  5. An inconsistent system would not be a valid counterexample to that particular claim, because it violates the assumption of consistency.

11.3 True/false answers need mathematical evidence

SEE THE IDEA

A counterexample must meet the assumptions

Use one example to disprove a universal claim, not to establish it.

ClaimEvidence required
True for all AA general proof covering all allowed A
False for some AOne allowed A for which it fails
If and only ifBoth logical directions

  1. Consider 'A matrix with a pivot in every column has columns spanning its codomain.' It is false for

    A=[100100]A = [1,0;0,1;0,0]

  2. Each column has a pivot,

  3. but

    b=(0,0,1)b = (0,0,1)

    cannot be produced.

  4. The missing row pivot is the precise reason.

  5. The counterexample states dimensions, verifies the hypothesis, and exhibits a failing output.

  1. Now consider 'If

    Ax=0Ax = 0

    has a nontrivial solution, then the columns of A are dependent.' This is true by the definition of column dependence: Ax is the weighted column combination, and a nontrivial x gives weights not all zero.

  2. The explanation names the definition and connects both pieces of language.

11.4 Integrated transfer practice

TRY IT YOURSELF · G1

G1. Let A = [120011][1,2,0;0,1,1]. For b = (3,2), solve Ax = b; solve Ax = 0; decide spanning, independence, onto, and one-to-one. Explain how the solution sets are related.

Show Detailed Solution · G1

G1.

Solve the system for a general output (3,2)

x1+2x2=3x_1 + 2x_2 = 3
x2+x3=2x_2 + x_3 = 2

Choose x2x₂ and calculate the other coordinates

x2=tx_2 = t
x1=3−2tx_1 = 3 - 2t
x3=2−tx_3 = 2 - t
x=[302]+t[−21−1]x = [3;0;2] + t[-2;1;-1]

Check both equations for every t

(3−2t)+2t=3(3-2t) + 2t = 3
t+(2−t)=2t + (2-t) = 2

Solve with zero on the right instead

x1+2x2=0x_1 + 2x_2 = 0
x2+x3=0x_2 + x_3 = 0
x=t[−21−1]x = t[-2;1;-1]

The homogeneous directions are unchanged. The earlier solution set starts at (3,0,2), so it is a translated copy.

Read spanning and onto from the rows

Column 1 pivots in row 1; column 2 pivots in row 2. Every row has a pivot. Thus the columns span ℝ2ℝ² and the map is onto ℝ2ℝ².

Read independence and one-to-one from the columns

3−2=13 - 2 = 1

Three columns but only two pivots leave one free weight. For example, t = 1 gives the nonzero homogeneous input (−2,1,−1). The columns are dependent and the map is not one-to-one.

FINAL ANSWER
Ax=(3,2):x=[302]+t[−21−1]Ax = (3,2): x = [3;0;2] + t[-2;1;-1]
Ax=0:x=t[−21−1]Ax = 0: x = t[-2;1;-1]

All t are real. The columns span ℝ2ℝ² but are dependent. T is onto and not one-to-one.

TRY IT YOURSELF · G2

G2. Let S(x1x₁,x2x₂) = (x1x₁ + 2x2x₂,x2x₂) and R(x1x₁,x2x₂) = (-x2x₂,x1x₁). Find the matrix of R after S, compute the image of (1,2), and find an inverse rule.

Show Detailed Solution · G2

G2.

Record each rule in the correct action order

(a,b)↦(a+2b,b)↦(−b,a+2b)(a,b) ↦ (a+2b,b) ↦ (-b,a+2b)

Read the composite coefficients

Apply the rule to (1,2)

(−2,1+2(2))=(−2,5)(-2,1+2(2)) = (-2,5)

Solve the output equations to undo the map

y1=−by_1 = -b
b=−y1b = -y_1
y2=a+2by_2 = a + 2b
a=y2−2(−y1)=2y1+y2a = y_2 - 2(-y_1) = 2y_1 + y_2

Check both matrix products

[0−112][21−10]=[1001][0,-1;1,2][2,1;-1,0] = [1,0;0,1]
[21−10][0−112]=[1001][2,1;-1,0][0,-1;1,2] = [1,0;0,1]

The products can also be checked entry by entry: the off-diagonal cancellations are 2 − 2 and −2 + 2; the diagonal entries are 1.

Undo the numerical output

(2(−2)+5,−(−2))=(1,2)(2(-2)+5,-(-2)) = (1,2)
FINAL ANSWER

The composite sends (a,b) to (−b,a + 2b). Its inverse sends (y1y₁,y2y₂) to (2y1y₁ + y2y₂,−y1y₁).

TRY IT YOURSELF · G3

G3. Suppose A is 3 × 3 and for every b ∈ ℝ3ℝ^3 there is at least one solution of Ax = b. Prove that the solution is always unique and A is invertible. Explain which part of the reasoning uses the fact that A is square.

Show Detailed Solution · G3

G3.

Given and goal

A is 3 × 3, and Ax = b can be solved for every b in ℝ3ℝ³. We must prove that each solution is unique and that A is invertible.

Convert existence into row information

The all-right-hand-side existence theorem gives a pivot in every coefficient row. Three rows therefore mean three pivots.

Use the fact that A is square

Those three pivots occupy three different columns. Since there are exactly three columns, every column is a pivot column. There are no free variables.

Conclude uniqueness and invertibility

Consistency is given for every b. With no free variables, each such system has exactly one solution. In RREF every column now has its own leading 1 and zeros elsewhere, so RREF(A) is I3I₃.

RREF(A)=I3RREF(A) = I_3

The inverse theorem says a square matrix reducible to I is invertible.

Identify where squareness was essential

For a 3 × 4 matrix, three row pivots would leave a fourth column without a pivot. Existence would still hold for every three-entry b, but uniqueness would fail.

FINAL ANSWER

Every Ax = b has exactly one solution, and A is invertible.

Every Ax = b has exactly one solution, and A is invertible.

chapters.title: 13. Glossary, formulas, and theorem reference
chapters.html:
13.1 Glossary

SEE THE IDEA

Use the words as labels for visible features

Choose a term, then connect it to the matrices, systems, or maps where it is used.

  1. Pivot: a leading location
  2. Free variable: a coefficient column without a pivot
  3. Span: every obtainable weighted sum
  4. Inverse: an operation that undoes A
Augmented matrix
coefficient columns together with one or more right-hand-side columns.
Basic variable
a variable whose coefficient column contains a pivot.
Coefficient
a fixed number multiplying an unknown.
Codomain
declared output space of a function.
Consistent
possessing at least one solution.
Dependent
admitting a zero combination with weights not all zero.
Domain
allowed input space.
Echelon form
zero rows last, leading entries moving right, zeros below leading entries.
Elementary matrix
identity after one elementary row operation.
Equivalent systems
systems with the same solution set.
Free variable
a nonpivot coefficient variable that can be chosen arbitrarily in a consistent system.
Homogeneous
having zero right-hand side.
Identity matrix
square matrix with diagonal 1 and off-diagonal 0.
Image
output of a specified input.
Independent
only the all-zero weights combine the vectors to zero.
Inverse
square matrix undoing another matrix in both multiplication orders.
Linear combination
weighted sum of vectors.
Linear transformation
function preserving addition and scalar multiplication.
Matrix dimensions
rows × columns.
Nontrivial solution
a solution vector other than zero.
One-to-one
different inputs always have different outputs.
Onto
every codomain vector is attained.
Parametric vector form
a fixed vector plus arbitrary scalar multiples of fixed direction vectors.
Particular solution
any one fixed solution of Ax = b.
Pivot column
original matrix column corresponding to a leading entry in its echelon form.
Pivot position
location corresponding to a leading 1 in RREF.
Range
set of outputs actually attained.
Reduced echelon form
echelon form with leading 1s, each alone as a nonzero entry in its column.
Row equivalent
connected by elementary row operations.
Scalar
real-number multiplier in this book.
Singular
square and not invertible.
Solution set
all lists satisfying every equation.
Span
all linear combinations of the listed generators.
Standard matrix
matrix whose columns are images of standard basis vectors.
Transpose
matrix with rows and columns exchanged.
Trivial solution
zero input in a homogeneous system.

13.3 Theorem correspondence

SEE THE IDEA

The section identifies the theorem numbering

Chapter 2 restarts its theorem numbers. Use the course section and theorem number together.

  1. Identify the topic
  2. Read the exact theorem and assumptions
  3. Check the physical source-page reference

  1. Combined PDF Chapter 1 numbers its theorems continuously: Theorem 1 is uniqueness of RREF (PDF page 13);

  2. Theorem 2 is consistency and uniqueness (26);

  3. Theorem 3 equates system, vector, and matrix equations (39);

  4. Theorem 4 equates row pivots, spanning, and existence for every b (40);

  5. Theorem 5 gives matrix-vector linearity (42-43);

  6. Theorem 6 describes translated homogeneous solution sets (52);

  7. Theorem 7 characterizes dependence (58-59);

  8. Theorem 8 treats more vectors than entries (61-62);

  9. Theorem 9 treats collections containing zero (62);

  10. Theorem 10 gives the standard matrix (71-72);

  11. Theorem 11 equates one-to-one behavior with the trivial homogeneous solution (78-79);

  12. Theorem 12 equates onto with spanning and one-to-one with independence (79).

  1. The Chapter 2 numbering restarts: Theorem 1 states addition and scalar laws (82-83);

  2. Theorem 2 states product laws (87-88);

  3. Theorem 3 states transpose identities (89-90);

  4. Theorem 4 gives the 2 × 2 inverse condition (92);

  5. Theorem 5 gives the unique solution A−1A^(-1)b (92);

  6. Theorem 6 gives inverse identities (93);

  7. Theorem 7 equates invertibility with row equivalence to identity (96-97).

  8. Use both the course section and theorem number to identify a theorem unambiguously.

13.4 Common mistakes and their repairs

SEE THE IDEA

Name the distinction that prevents the mistake

Many errors swap two similar-sounding conditions.

Keep separateWhy
Rows / columnsRows ask existence; columns ask uniqueness
Zero row / contradictory row0 = 0 is harmless; 0 = 1 is impossible
AB / BAActions occur in a different order
A span / one vector in itA set is not one of its members

  1. A pivot in every row answers an existence question for all right-hand sides.

  2. A pivot in every column answers uniqueness of inputs.

  3. Write the words 'row/output/existence' and 'column/input/uniqueness' beside a rectangular matrix before deciding.

  1. A free coefficient variable yields infinitely many solutions only when the system is consistent.

  2. First search for an impossible row.

  3. A zero row

    0=00 = 0

    adds no constraint;

  4. a row

    0=10 = 1

    rules out all solutions.

  1. A vector equation uses the supplied vectors as columns, not rows.

  2. The unknown weights become input entries.

  3. Original pivot columns are found by their indices;

  4. reduced columns generally have different entries and should not be substituted as the original vectors.

  1. A zero vector in a collection guarantees dependence;

  2. a nonzero vector does not guarantee independence of a collection.

  3. A dependence relation needs weights not all zero.

  4. A theorem about all inputs needs a general proof;

  5. a failed universal statement needs only one valid counterexample.

  1. Matrix multiplication is row by column, not entrywise.

  2. Inner dimensions must match.

  3. You may regroup associative products but may not reorder factors.

  4. Transpose and inverse reverse the order of products.

  5. Cancellation needs an invertible factor in the correct position.

  1. Inversion requires a square matrix.

  2. For a 2 × 2 matrix check ad - bc before dividing.

  3. For row reduction carry the whole identity block with every operation.

  4. Verify against the original A, especially when the source contains a typographical discrepancy.

chapters.title: 14. Sources, scope, and verification notes
chapters.html:
14.1 Section correspondence

The supplied Combined PDF has lecture sections at physical PDF pages 1-11 (1.1), 12-27 (1.2), 28-36 (1.3), 37-43 (1.4), 44-52 (1.5), 53-62 (1.7), 63-70 (1.8), 71-79 (1.9), 80-90 (2.1), and 91-100 (2.2). Selected worked answers occupy pages 101-116. These are physical PDF page numbers, not the printed slide numbers.

The Exercise PDF pages are mapped in the companion workbook. Its full readable question inventory is solved there, with the two truncated question continuations identified. Section 1.4 questions 33-34 and Section 1.9 questions 31-32 are mentioned by printed group directions but their statements are absent from the supplied scans; they are not silently invented. The later exam cheat sheet is outside these two volumes.

14.2 Source discrepancies and assumptions

  1. The inverse example mismatch on Combined PDF page 98 is preserved and explained in Chapter 10, with both matrices independently inverted.

  2. The nonhomogeneous slide on page 48 labels its augmented block [A 0] although the actual constants are

    b=(7,−1,−4)b = (7,-1,-4)

  3. the computation is of [A b].

  4. The phrase 'plane' for s u + t v requires u,v independent if it is to mean a genuine two-dimensional plane;

  5. dependent directions instead produce a line or {0}.

  6. Those assumptions are made explicit here.

  1. All source pages were visually reviewed, alongside text extraction for the lectures.

  2. No missing exercise continuation has been reconstructed from a different edition.

  3. Original pedagogical explanations, diagrams, practice questions, and their answers were authored for this resource.

  4. Mathematical identities were justified with the assumptions stated.

  5. Exact computational checks accompany generated reductions: the row-operation product maps the original matrix to its reduced matrix;

  6. particular and direction vectors satisfy the original systems;

  7. products agree by two constructions;

  8. inverse products equal I in both orders.

  9. These checks support arithmetic accuracy without replacing the written reasoning.

14.3 A complete solution is more than a final vector

  1. A university solution identifies the mathematical request, records the data in the right form, shows valid operations, interprets the pivots or parameters, and returns to the question's wording.

  2. Verification tests the answer against the original data.

  3. The purpose of this book is to make that chain understandable enough that the method can be carried to an unfamiliar problem.

exercises.title: Show that every (h,k) is in Span{u,v}
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Given

u = (2,−1), v = (2,1), and the target (h,k) is arbitrary in ℝ2ℝ².

What must be shown

Show that every (h,k) is in Span{u,v}

Main idea

Find weights in terms of h and k, then substitute them. Fixed nonzero denominators allow every target.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Show that every (h,k) is in Span{u,v}.

Words used in this question

The span is the set of every weighted sum of the supplied vectors. Membership asks whether weights can produce this particular target.

Given and what must be shown

u=[2−1]u = [2;-1]
v=[21]v = [2;1]
αu+βv=[hk]αu+βv = [h;k]

h,k are any real target coordinates. We must find weights α,β for every such target. This is what spanning all of ℝ2ℝ² means.

Translate the weighted sum into coordinate equations

2α+2β=h2α+2β = h
−α+β=k-α+β = k

Solve the second equation for β

β=k+αβ = k+α

Add α to both sides. Substitute this expression for β in the first equation.

Solve carefully for α

2α+2(k+α)=h2α+2(k+α) = h
2α+2k+2α=h2α+2k+2α = h
4α+2k=h4α+2k = h
4α=h−2k4α = h-2k
α=(h−2k)4=h4−k2α = (h-2k)/4 = h/4-k/2

Then calculate β

β=k+h4−k2β = k+h/4-k/2
β=h4+k2β = h/4+k/2

Verify the first coordinate

2α+2β=2(h4−k2)+2(h4+k2)2α+2β = 2(h/4-k/2)+2(h/4+k/2)
2α+2β=h2−k+h2+k=h2α+2β = h/2-k+h/2+k = h

Verify the second coordinate

−α+β=−(h4−k2)+(h4+k2)-α+β = -(h/4-k/2)+(h/4+k/2)
−α+β=−h4+k2+h4+k2=k-α+β = -h/4+k/2+h/4+k/2 = k
FINAL ANSWER
α=h4−k2α = h/4-k/2
β=h4+k2β = h/4+k/2

The fixed denominators 4 and 2 are nonzero. The weights exist for every real h,k, so u and v span ℝ2ℝ².

  1. The second row of

  2. Applying R2R₂ ← R2R₂ + 3R1R₁ to [A | b] gives [00b2+3b1][0,0 | b₂ + 3b₁].

  5. For example

    b=(0,1)b = (0,1)

    fails,

  7. Conversely, when the condition holds, the first equation

    2x1−x2=b12x₁ - x₂ = b₁

    always has solutions.

Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Your task. h for span membership and for dependence.

Words used in this question

The span is the set of every weighted sum of the supplied vectors. Membership asks whether weights can produce this particular target.

Independence means the only weights producing the zero vector are all zero. A nonzero collection of weights producing zero is a dependence relation.

Part (a): express v3v₃ using v1v₁ and v2v₂

v3=αv1+βv2v_3 = αv_1+βv_2
α−3β=2α-3β = 2
−3α+10β=−7-3α+10β = -7

Solve the first two coordinate equations

α=2+3βα = 2+3β
−3(2+3β)+10β=−7-3(2+3β)+10β = -7
−6−9β+10β=−7-6-9β+10β = -7
β=−1β = -1
α=2+3(−1)=−1α = 2+3(-1) = -1

Compute the third coordinate these weights force

h=2α−6βh = 2α-6β
h=2(−1)−6(−1)h = 2(-1)-6(-1)
h=−2+6=4h = -2+6 = 4

Part (b): check the first pair before using the span test

A zero combination of v1v₁,v2v₂ gives these same first two equations with zero right sides:

α−3β=0α-3β = 0
−3α+10β=0-3α+10β = 0
α=3βα = 3β
−9β+10β=β=0-9β+10β = β = 0
α=0α = 0

Only zero weights work, so the pair is independent. Therefore adding v3v₃ creates dependence exactly when v3v₃ is in their span.

Show an actual nonzero relation at h = 4

v3=−v1−v2v_3 = -v_1-v_2
v1+v2+v3=0v_1+v_2+v_3 = 0

The weights (1,1,1) are not all zero. This is a nontrivial relation.

FINAL ANSWER

(a) Membership holds exactly for h = 4. (b) The triple is dependent exactly for h = 4. The conclusion in part (b) uses the independence of the original pair.

The span is the set of every weighted sum of the supplied vectors. Membership asks whether weights can produce this particular target.

2v1+v2=02v_1+v_2 = 0

The two vectors are already dependent. Every combination of them is a multiple of v1v₁, so they span a line.

At h = −6 all three coordinates match, so membership holds. Any other h makes the third coordinate fail.

The weights 2,1,0 are not all zero. This works for every h because v3v₃ has weight zero.

The calculation below starts with 2 rows. Its 2 columns before the divider record the coefficients; the 1 column after the divider record the right-hand side.

Read the actual first row

(1)x1+(1)x2=3(1)x_1 + (1)x_2 = 3
Words used in this question

A coefficient is the number multiplying an unknown. A missing term has coefficient 0.

In a row staircase, a leading entry is the first nonzero entry when reading a nonzero row from left to right. Its position is a pivot position. A pivot coefficient column determines a basic coordinate; a nonpivot coefficient column allows a free coordinate.

Use the coefficients of T(x1x₁,x2x₂) = (x1x₁ + x2x₂,4x1x₁ + 5x2x₂) as the standard matrix, then solve the requested output equation.

  1. Each coefficient column corresponds to one unknown;

  2. the column after the vertical divider records the right-hand sides.

  3. We use reversible row operations to reveal the constraints.

The starting matrix is:

[113458]

Step 1: R2R_2 ← R2R_2 + (-4)R1R_1. Add -4 times row 1 to row 2. This cancels the entry in the pivot column while preserving the solutions. All other rows stay as displayed.

Before
[113458]
After
[11301−4]

Lavender: affected row. Sage: pivot used.

Calculate every entry in the changed row

Multiply each entry of old row 1 by -4, then add it to the matching entry of old row 2. The other row is retained.

Row 2, column 1
4+(−4)(1)=4−4=04 + (-4)(1) = 4 - 4 = 0
Row 2, column 2

exercises.title: True/false: A linear map is determined by its action on identity columns
exercises.question:
Mark this statement True or False. Justify your answer.

A linear transformation T: ℝnℝⁿ → ℝᵐ is completely determined by its effect on the columns of the n × n identity matrix.
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Your task. True/false: A linear map is determined by its action on identity columns.

Words used in this question

Linearity means addition and scalar weights are preserved. A scalar is a single real-number multiplier.

Read the exact statement above. The verdict below concerns all of its assumptions; the reason or counterexample is part of the answer.

True. Every input is a combination of those standard basis columns. Linearity applies the same combination to their known images, so no other choices of outputs remain.

FINAL ANSWER

True. A linear map is determined by its action on identity columns

exercises.title: True/false: Unique output for each input makes a mapping one-to-one
exercises.question:
Mark this statement True or False. Justify your answer.

A mapping T: ℝnℝⁿ → ℝᵐ is one-to-one if each vector in ℝnℝⁿ maps onto a unique vector in ℝᵐ.
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Your task. True/false: Unique output for each input makes a mapping one-to-one.

Words used in this question

One-to-one means different inputs never give the same output. For a linear map this is equivalent to only the zero input producing zero.

Read the exact statement above. The verdict below concerns all of its assumptions; the reason or counterexample is part of the answer.

False. Every function already has a unique output for each input. One-to-one additionally prohibits two different inputs from sharing an output. The zero map is a function with unique output 0 for every input but is not one-to-one.

FINAL ANSWER

False. Unique output for each input makes a mapping one-to-one

Mark this statement True or False. Justify your answer.

A mapping T: ℝnℝⁿ → ℝᵐ is onto ℝᵐ if every vector x in ℝnℝⁿ maps onto some vector in ℝᵐ.
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Your task. True/false: A map is onto if each input has some output.

Words used in this question

Onto means every vector in the stated codomain can be reached. It requires a pivot in every coefficient row.

Read the exact statement above. The verdict below concerns all of its assumptions; the reason or counterexample is part of the answer.

  1. False. That is a basic property of a function, not the onto condition.

  2. Onto requires every vector in the codomain to be attained.

  3. Projection

    (a,b)↦(a,0)(a,b) ↦ (a,0)

False. A map is onto if each input has some output

The standard matrix of a linear transformation from ℝ2ℝ² to ℝ2ℝ² that reflects points through the horizontal axis, the vertical axis, or the origin has the form [a00d][a,0;0,d], where a and d are ±1.

Independence means the only weights producing the zero vector are all zero. A nonzero collection of weights producing zero is a dependence relation.

Homogeneous means the right side is the zero vector. The zero input always works; nontrivial means a different, nonzero input.

    n≤mn ≤ m

exercises.title: Prove left and right distributive laws
exercises.question: Assume each matrix expression is defined: matrix and vector sizes match appropriately.
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Given

The matrices have compatible sizes for each stated sum and product.

What must be shown

Prove left and right distributive laws

Main idea

Compare the same (i,j) entry on both sides. Distribute ordinary real-number multiplication inside that entry. Here i names an output row, j an output column, and k the matching inner-entry position. The symbol Σ means add the term for every allowed k. An entry aijaᵢⱼ is the number in row i, column j.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Prove left and right distributive laws.

  1. For left distributivity, entry i,j of A(B + C) is Σ over k of aika_{ik}(bkjb_{kj} + ckjc_{kj}).

  2. Real distributivity turns this into Σ aika_{ik}bkjb_{kj} + Σ aika_{ik}ckjc_{kj}, the i,j entry of AB + AC.

  3. For right distributivity, entry i,j of (B + C)A is

    Σ(bik+cik)akj=Σbikakj+ΣcikakjΣ (b_{ik} + c_{ik})a_{kj} = Σ b_{ik}a_{kj} + Σ c_{ik}a_{kj}

    , the i,j entry of BA + CA.

  4. The matrices on each side have the same size by the stated compatibility assumption.

  5. Agreement of every entry proves both identities.

FINAL ANSWER

A(B + C) = AB + AC and (B + C)A = BA + CA, for the stated compatible sizes.

exercises.title: Show AD = I forces D = A^(-1) when A is invertible
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Given

A is invertible and AD = I.

What must be shown

Show AD = I forces D = A−1A^(-1) when A is invertible

Main idea

Multiply on the left by A−1A⁻¹ so that A−1A⁻¹A becomes an adjacent inverse pair.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Show AD = I forces D = A−1A^(-1) when A is invertible.

  1. Left-multiply

    AD=IAD = I

    by A−1A^(-1).

  2. Associativity gives

    (A−1A)D=A−1I(A^(-1)A)D = A^(-1)I

  3. hence

    ID=A−1I D = A^(-1)

    and

    D=A−1D = A^(-1)

  4. The assumption that A is invertible provides the legal left multiplier.

  5. The proof does not cancel A informally.

FINAL ANSWER

D = A−1A⁻¹.

exercises.title: True/false: An inverse satisfies both AB = I and BA = I
exercises.question:
Mark this statement True or False. Justify your answer.

In order for a matrix B to be the inverse of A, both equations AB = I and BA = I must be true.
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Your task. True/false: An inverse satisfies both AB = I and BA = I.

Words used in this question

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

Read the exact statement above. The verdict below concerns all of its assumptions; the reason or counterexample is part of the answer.

  1. True. These are the two defining identities for the inverse of a square matrix.

  2. Both hold for the unique inverse.

  3. A theorem may allow one to infer the other for square matrices,

  4. but that does not change the defining conditions.

FINAL ANSWER

True. An inverse satisfies both AB = I and BA = I

exercises.title: True/false: Inverse of a product keeps the factor order
exercises.question:
Mark this statement True or False. Justify your answer.

A product of invertible n × n matrices is invertible, and the inverse of the product is the product of their inverses in the same order.
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Your task. True/false: Inverse of a product keeps the factor order.

Words used in this question

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

Read the exact statement above. The verdict below concerns all of its assumptions; the reason or counterexample is part of the answer.

  1. False. For invertible

    A,B,(AB)−1=B−1A−1A,B, (AB)^(-1) = B^(-1)A^(-1)

  2. Multiplying AB by this reverse-order candidate brings B beside B−1B^(-1) and then A beside A−1A^(-1).

  3. Keeping the order generally leaves uncancelled interleaved factors.

FINAL ANSWER

False. Inverse of a product keeps the factor order

exercises.title: True/false: A^(-1)B^(-1) is the inverse of AB
exercises.question:

Your task. True/false: A−1A^(-1)B−1B^(-1) is the inverse of AB.

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

Read the exact statement above. The verdict below concerns all of its assumptions; the reason or counterexample is part of the answer.

  1. False. It is the inverse of BA.

  2. As a numerical check, take

    A=[1101],B=[1002]A = [1,1;0,1], B = [1,0;0,2]

  3. Then

    (AB)−1=[1−1012](AB)^(-1) = [1,-1;0,1/2]

    A−1B−1=[1−12012]A^(-1)B^(-1) = [1,-1/2;0,1/2]

  5. They are unequal.

False. A−1A^(-1)B−1B^(-1) is the inverse of AB

exercises.title: True/false: The inverse of A^(-1) is A

Mark this statement True or False. Justify your answer.

If A is invertible, then the inverse of A−1A^(-1) is A itself.
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Your task. True/false: The inverse of A−1A^(-1) is A.

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

Read the exact statement above. The verdict below concerns all of its assumptions; the reason or counterexample is part of the answer.

    and

exercises.title: True/false: ab - cd ≠ 0 ensures a 2 × 2 inverse
exercises.question:
Mark this statement True or False. Justify your answer.

If A = [abcd][a,b;c,d] and ab − cd ≠ 0, then A is invertible.
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Your task. True/false: ab - cd ≠ 0 ensures a 2 × 2 inverse.

Words used in this question

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

Read the exact statement above. The verdict below concerns all of its assumptions; the reason or counterexample is part of the answer.

  1. False. The determinant is ad - bc.

  2. For

    A=[1224],ab−cd=2−8=−6≠0A = [1,2;2,4], ab - cd = 2 - 8 = -6 ≠ 0

  3. but

    ad−bc=4−4=0ad - bc = 4 - 4 = 0

  4. The columns are proportional,

  5. so this is a singular counterexample satisfying the stated inequality.

False. ab - cd ≠ 0 ensures a 2 × 2 inverse

exercises.title: True/false: ad = bc makes the 2 × 2 matrix singular
exercises.question:
Mark this statement True or False. Justify your answer.

If A = [abcd][a,b;c,d] and ad = bc, then A is not invertible.
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Your task. True/false: ad = bc makes the 2 × 2 matrix singular.

Words used in this question

Homogeneous means the right side is the zero vector. The zero input always works; nontrivial means a different, nonzero input.

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

Read the exact statement above. The verdict below concerns all of its assumptions; the reason or counterexample is part of the answer.

  1. True. The determinant ad - bc is zero.

  2. If the first row is nonzero, (-b,a) is a nonzero homogeneous solution;

  3. if it is zero, a nonzero solution is obtained from the remaining row or any vector if both rows vanish.

  4. Thus the transformation cannot have a two-sided inverse.

FINAL ANSWER

True. ad = bc makes the 2 × 2 matrix singular

exercises.title: True/false: Invertibility ensures consistency for every b
exercises.question:
Mark this statement True or False. Justify your answer.

If A is an invertible n × n matrix, then the equation Ax = b is consistent for each b in ℝnℝⁿ.
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Your task. True/false: Invertibility ensures consistency for every b.

Words used in this question

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

Read the exact statement above. The verdict below concerns all of its assumptions; the reason or counterexample is part of the answer.

  1. True. For any b, choose

    x=A−1bx = A^(-1)b

  2. Then

    Ax=AA−1b=bAx = AA^(-1)b = b

    , constructing a solution.

  3. The same inverse also proves uniqueness, although this statement asks only consistency.

True. Invertibility ensures consistency for every b

exercises.title: True/false: Row reducing A to identity proves invertibility
exercises.question:
Mark this statement True or False. Justify your answer.

If A can be row reduced to the identity matrix, then A must be invertible.
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Your task. True/false: Row reducing A to identity proves invertibility.

Words used in this question

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

Read the exact statement above. The verdict below concerns all of its assumptions; the reason or counterexample is part of the answer.

  1. True. The elementary row operations have an invertible product E with

    EA=IEA = I

  2. Applying them to I gives E, and

    A=E−1A = E^(-1)

  3. so

    E=A−1E = A^(-1)

  4. This is the Gauss-Jordan inverse theorem for square A.

FINAL ANSWER

True. Row reducing A to identity proves invertibility

exercises.title: True/false: Every elementary matrix is invertible
exercises.question:
Mark this statement True or False. Justify your answer.

Each elementary matrix is invertible.
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Your task. True/false: Every elementary matrix is invertible.

Words used in this question

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

Read the exact statement above. The verdict below concerns all of its assumptions; the reason or counterexample is part of the answer.

  1. True. Its single row operation can be undone: swap again, scale by the reciprocal nonzero scalar, or add the opposite multiple of the retained row.

  2. The matrix for that reverse operation is its inverse.

FINAL ANSWER

True. Every elementary matrix is invertible

exercises.title: True/false: Operations reducing A to I also reduce A^(-1) to I
exercises.question:
Mark this statement True or False. Justify your answer.

If A is invertible, the elementary row operations that reduce A to the identity InIₙ also reduce A−1A^(-1) to InIₙ.
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Your task. True/false: Operations reducing A to I also reduce A−1A^(-1) to I.

Read the exact statement above. The verdict below concerns all of its assumptions; the reason or counterexample is part of the answer.

  1. False. Their combined left multiplier is A−1A^(-1),

  2. so applied to A−1A^(-1) they give A−2A^(-2), not generally I.

  3. For

    A=2IA = 2I

    , the reduction scales rows by 121/2;

  4. applying it to

    A−1=(12)IA^(-1) = (1/2)I

    gives (141/4)I.

  5. The actual theorem says the operations send I to A−1A^(-1).

False. Operations reducing A to I also reduce A−1A^(-1) to I

exercises.title: Unique matrix solution of AX = B
exercises.solution:
Independently derived and cross-checked against the selected supplied solution on Combined PDF page 115.

Given

A is invertible of size n × n; B is n × p.

What must be shown

Unique matrix solution of AX = B

Main idea

Construct X = A−1A⁻¹B for existence. Apply the same inverse to any other solution for uniqueness.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Unique matrix solution of AX = B.

  1. Existence: set

    X=A−1BX = A^(-1)B

  2. Dimensions are

    (n×n)(n×p)=n×p(n × n)(n × p) = n × p

    , and

    AX=A(A−1B)=(AA−1)B=BAX = A(A^(-1)B) = (AA^(-1))B = B

  3. Uniqueness: if Y is any matrix satisfying

    AY=BAY = B

    , left-multiply by A−1A^(-1) to get

    Y=A−1B=XY = A^(-1)B = X

  4. This proves every column system at once and does not require B to be square.

FINAL ANSWER

X = A−1A⁻¹B is the unique solution; B may be rectangular.

exercises.title: Why [A B] reduction computes A^(-1)B
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Given

A is invertible; B is any compatible n × p block. Row operations turn [A | B] into [I | X].

What must be shown

Why [A B] reduction computes A−1A^(-1)B

Main idea

The same row-operation product multiplies both blocks on the left. On A it acts as A−1A⁻¹, so it does the same to B.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Why [A B] reduction computes A−1A^(-1)B.

Words used in this question

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

  1. Each elementary row operation left-multiplies every block by the same elementary matrix.

  2. Their total product E sends A to I,

  3. so

    EA=IEA = I

    and

    E=A−1E = A^(-1)

  4. Consequently the final right block is

    X=EB=A−1BX = EB = A^(-1)B

  5. This explains why carrying B through elimination works directly without separately forming and multiplying the inverse.

  6. Dimensions permit any n × p right block B.

FINAL ANSWER

The final right block is X = A−1A⁻¹B.

exercises.title: Cancellation with invertible A and failure without it
exercises.solution:
Independently derived and cross-checked against the selected supplied solution on Combined PDF page 115.

Given

AB = AC, A is invertible, and B,C are compatible.

What must be shown

Cancellation with invertible A and failure without it

Main idea

Put A−1A⁻¹ beside A on the left. Then examine a singular counterexample to see why the hypothesis matters.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Cancellation with invertible A and failure without it.

  1. If

    AB=ACAB = AC

    and A is invertible, left-multiply by A−1A^(-1).

  2. Associativity gives

    B=CB = C

  3. In general this is false for singular A: take

    A=[1000],B=[0001],C=0A = [1,0;0,0], B = [0,0;0,1], C = 0

  4. Both products are zero,

  5. but

    B≠CB ≠ C

  6. This counterexample satisfies matching dimensions and directly shows why invertibility matters.

FINAL ANSWER

B = C when A is invertible. The stated conclusion fails in general for singular A, as the displayed counterexample shows.

exercises.title: Cancel an invertible right factor
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Given

(B − C)D = 0, and D is invertible.

What must be shown

Cancel an invertible right factor

Main idea

Use D−1D⁻¹ on the right, where it can be adjacent to D. A left multiplier would not generally cancel that factor.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Cancel an invertible right factor.

Words used in this question

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

  1. From

    (B−C)D=0(B - C)D = 0

    , multiply both sides on the right by D−1D^(-1).

  2. This gives

    (B−C)(DD−1)=0D−1(B - C)(DD^(-1)) = 0D^(-1)

  3. so

    B−C=0B - C = 0

    and hence

    B=CB = C

  4. Left-multiplication would not put D beside its inverse in general.

  5. Only D needs to be invertible;

  6. B and C need not be square.

FINAL ANSWER

B = C. Only D must be invertible for this right-side cancellation.

exercises.title: Produce an inverse for ABC
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Given

A, B, and C are invertible square matrices of the same size.

What must be shown

Produce an inverse for ABC

Main idea

Undo the rightmost action last: the candidate inverse is C−1C⁻¹B−1B⁻¹A−1A⁻¹. Verify both orders.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Produce an inverse for ABC.

Words used in this question

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

  1. Choose

    D=C−1B−1A−1D = C^(-1)B^(-1)A^(-1)

  2. Then

    (ABC)D=AB(CC−1)B−1A−1=A(BB−1)A−1=I(ABC)D = AB(CC^(-1))B^(-1)A^(-1) = A(BB^(-1))A^(-1) = I

  3. Similarly

    D(ABC)=C−1B−1(A−1A)BC=C−1(B−1B)C=ID(ABC) = C^(-1)B^(-1)(A^(-1)A)BC = C^(-1)(B^(-1)B)C = I

  4. Associativity permits these regroupings without moving factors.

  5. Thus D is the inverse by definition.

FINAL ANSWER

The inverse of ABC is C−1C⁻¹B−1B⁻¹A−1A⁻¹, with factors in reverse order.

exercises.title: B and AB invertible imply A invertible
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Given

B and AB are invertible n × n matrices.

What must be shown

B and AB invertible imply A invertible

Main idea

Write C = AB, so A = CB−1B⁻¹. A product of invertible factors has an inverse in reverse order.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. B and AB invertible imply A invertible.

Words used in this question

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

  1. Let

    C=ABC = AB

  2. Since B is invertible, right-multiplication yields

    A=CB−1A = CB^(-1)

  3. Both factors on the right are invertible,

  4. so A is invertible and its inverse is B C−1C^(-1).

  5. Check

    A(BC−1)=CB−1BC−1=IA(B C^(-1)) = CB^(-1)B C^(-1) = I

    and

    (BC−1)A=BC−1CB−1=I(B C^(-1))A = B C^(-1)C B^(-1) = I

  6. This produces the inverse rather than assuming cancellation alone proves it.

FINAL ANSWER

A is invertible, with inverse B(AB)⁻¹.

exercises.title: Solve AB = BC for A
exercises.solution:
Independently derived and cross-checked against the selected supplied solution on Combined PDF page 115.

Given

A, B, C are square, B is invertible, and AB = BC.

What must be shown

Solve AB = BC for A

Main idea

Right multiplication by B−1B⁻¹ removes the B attached to A; it does not permit commuting B with C.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Solve AB = BC for A.

  1. Right-multiply by B−1B^(-1) to obtain

    ABB−1=BCB−1ABB^(-1) = BCB^(-1)

  2. hence

    A=BCB−1A = BCB^(-1)

  3. Substituting back gives

    AB=BCB−1B=BCAB = BCB^(-1)B = BC

    , proving the formula meets the original equation.

  4. The factor order is essential;

  5. one cannot simplify to

    A=CA = C

    unless an extra commuting relation is known.

FINAL ANSWER

A = BCB−1B⁻¹.

exercises.title: Solve A = PBP^(-1) for B
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Given

P is invertible and A = PBP−1P⁻¹.

What must be shown

Solve A = PBP−1P^(-1) for B

Main idea

Remove the left P with a left P−1P⁻¹, and remove the right P−1P⁻¹ with a right P.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Solve A = PBP−1P^(-1) for B.

Words used in this question

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

  1. Left-multiply by P−1P^(-1) and right-multiply by P.

  2. The result is

    P−1AP=P−1PBP−1P=BP^(-1)AP = P^(-1)PBP^(-1)P = B

  3. Thus

    B=P−1APB = P^(-1)AP

  4. Substituting into PBP−1P^(-1) cancels the adjacent inverse pairs and returns A, validating the formula.

  5. Only P’s invertibility is needed for this rearrangement.

FINAL ANSWER

B = P−1P⁻¹AP.

exercises.title: Solve C^(-1)(A + X)B^(-1) = I
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Given

A, B, C are invertible n × n matrices; C−1C⁻¹(A + X)B−1B⁻¹ = I.

What must be shown

Solve C−1C^(-1)(A + X)B−1B^(-1) = I

Main idea

Undo the outer inverse factors on their own sides, leaving A + X = CB.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Solve C−1C^(-1)(A + X)B−1B^(-1) = I.

  1. Left-multiply by C, giving

    (A+X)B−1=C(A + X)B^(-1) = C

  2. Right-multiply by B to obtain

    A+X=CBA + X = CB

  3. Hence

    X=CB−AX = CB - A

  4. This matrix always exists with the stated matching sizes;

  5. X itself need not be invertible.

  6. Substitution gives

    C−1(CB)B−1=IC^(-1)(CB)B^(-1) = I

  7. so existence is proved and the reversible rearrangement also proves uniqueness.

FINAL ANSWER

X = CB − A is the solution.

exercises.title: Solve (A - AX)^(-1) = X^(-1)B
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Given

A, X, and A − AX are invertible n × n matrices, and (A − AX)⁻¹ = X−1X⁻¹B.

What must be shown

Solve (A - AX)^(-1) = X−1X^(-1)B

Main idea

First prove that B is invertible. Invert the equality in reverse factor order, then prove a new factor is invertible before using its inverse.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Solve (A - AX)^(-1) = X−1X^(-1)B.

Words used in this question

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

Given and the two goals

(A−AX)−1=X−1B(A - AX)^(-1) = X^(-1)B

A, X, and A − AX are invertible square matrices. First prove B is invertible. Then solve for X, justifying every inverse used.

Part (a): isolate B by multiplying on the left

X(A−AX)−1=XX−1BX(A-AX)^(-1) = XX^(-1)B
B=X(A−AX)−1B = X(A-AX)^(-1)

Both factors on the right are invertible by the hypotheses. Their product is invertible.

Write and justify the inverse of B

B−1=(A−AX)X−1B^(-1) = (A-AX)X^(-1)

The inverse of a product reverses factor order. Multiplying these two displayed products in either order cancels adjacent inverse pairs to give I.

Part (b): invert the original equality

A−AX=(X−1B)−1A - AX = (X^(-1)B)^(-1)
A−AX=B−1XA - AX = B^(-1)X

The right side must reverse order. B−1B⁻¹ is now legal because part (a) established invertibility.

Gather the terms containing X on the right

A=AX+B−1XA = AX + B^(-1)X
A=(A+B−1)XA = (A + B^(-1))X

Distribute on the right to check this factoring. No factors have been commuted.

Prove the new left factor is invertible before using it

A+B−1=AX−1A + B^(-1) = AX^(-1)

Multiply the preceding equality on the right by X−1X⁻¹. The result is a product of two invertible matrices, so A + B−1B⁻¹ is invertible.

Now isolate X legally

(A+B−1)−1A=X(A+B^(-1))^(-1)A = X

Check against the original identity

A=(A+B−1)XA = (A+B^(-1))X
A−AX=B−1XA - AX = B^(-1)X
(A−AX)−1=(B−1X)−1=X−1B(A-AX)^(-1) = (B^(-1)X)^(-1) = X^(-1)B

Factoring back and then inverting recovers the original equality under the stated hypotheses.

FINAL ANSWER
B−1=(A−AX)X−1B^(-1) = (A-AX)X^(-1)
X=(A+B−1)−1AX = (A+B^(-1))^(-1)A

exercises.title: Why are columns independent when A is invertible?
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Given

A is an invertible n × n matrix.

What must be shown

Why are columns independent when A is invertible?

Main idea

Apply A−1A⁻¹ to Ax = 0. If only zero weights produce zero, the columns are independent.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Why are columns independent when A is invertible?.

Words used in this question

Independence means the only weights producing the zero vector are all zero. A nonzero collection of weights producing zero is a dependence relation.

Homogeneous means the right side is the zero vector. The zero input always works; nontrivial means a different, nonzero input.

  1. If

    Ax=0Ax = 0

    , left-multiplying by A−1A^(-1) gives

    x=0x = 0

  2. Thus only the trivial weights combine the columns to zero, which is the definition of column independence.

  3. This directly connects invertibility to the homogeneous test without relying on a numerical reduction.

FINAL ANSWER

The columns of an invertible A are linearly independent.

exercises.title: Why do invertible columns span ℝ^n?
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Given

A is invertible of size n × n; b is an arbitrary target in ℝnℝⁿ.

What must be shown

Why do invertible columns span ℝnℝ^n?

Main idea

Use x = A−1A⁻¹b to build every target from the columns of A.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Why do invertible columns span ℝnℝ^n?.

Words used in this question

In a row staircase, a leading entry is the first nonzero entry when reading a nonzero row from left to right. Its position is a pivot position. A pivot coefficient column determines a basic coordinate; a nonpivot coefficient column allows a free coordinate.

The span is the set of every weighted sum of the supplied vectors. Membership asks whether weights can produce this particular target.

  1. For every

    b∈ℝn,x=A−1bb ∈ ℝ^n, x = A^(-1)b

    exists and satisfies

    Ax=bAx = b

  2. Hence every b is a linear combination of the columns, using the entries of that x as weights.

  3. By definition the columns span ℝnℝ^n.

  4. Equivalently, the every-right-hand-side existence theorem gives a pivot in every row.

FINAL ANSWER

The columns span all of ℝnℝⁿ.

exercises.title: Trivial homogeneous solution implies invertibility for square A
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Given

A is square and Ax = 0 has only the zero solution.

What must be shown

Trivial homogeneous solution implies invertibility for square A

Main idea

No free column is possible. In a square matrix all column pivots also fill all rows, so RREF is I.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Trivial homogeneous solution implies invertibility for square A.

Words used in this question

A coefficient is the number multiplying an unknown. A missing term has coefficient 0.

In a row staircase, a leading entry is the first nonzero entry when reading a nonzero row from left to right. Its position is a pivot position. A pivot coefficient column determines a basic coordinate; a nonpivot coefficient column allows a free coordinate.

Homogeneous means the right side is the zero vector. The zero input always works; nontrivial means a different, nonzero input.

  1. Only the trivial solution of

    Ax=0Ax = 0

    means no free coefficient variables,

  2. so all n columns have pivots.

  3. A has n rows as well,

  4. so its RREF has n leading 1s, one per row and column, and is InI_n.

  5. Thus A is row equivalent to InI_n.

  6. The Gauss-Jordan inverse theorem then proves invertibility.

  7. The same conclusion would fail for a tall nonsquare matrix,

  8. so squareness is explicitly used.

FINAL ANSWER

RREF(A) = InIₙ; hence A is invertible.

exercises.title: Every-right-hand-side existence implies invertibility for square A
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Given

A is square and Ax = b has a solution for every b in ℝnℝⁿ.

What must be shown

Every-right-hand-side existence implies invertibility for square A

Main idea

Every row has a pivot. Squareness makes the same count fill every column, producing I in RREF.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Every-right-hand-side existence implies invertibility for square A.

Words used in this question

In a row staircase, a leading entry is the first nonzero entry when reading a nonzero row from left to right. Its position is a pivot position. A pivot coefficient column determines a basic coordinate; a nonpivot coefficient column allows a free coordinate.

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

Onto means every vector in the stated codomain can be reached. It requires a pivot in every coefficient row.

  1. Solvability for each

    b∈ℝnb ∈ ℝ^n

    gives a pivot in every row of A.

  2. There are n rows and n columns,

  3. hence n pivots and no free columns.

  4. Its RREF is InI_n,

  5. so A is row equivalent to the identity and is invertible.

  6. A wide rectangular matrix can be onto without an ordinary two-sided inverse;

  7. the square hypothesis is required.

FINAL ANSWER

RREF(A) = InIₙ; hence A is invertible.

exercises.title: Why ad - bc = 0 prevents a 2 × 2 inverse
exercises.question: Prove Theorem 4 for A = [abcd][a,b;c,d].
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Given

A = [abcd][a,b;c,d] and ad − bc = 0.

What must be shown

Why ad - bc = 0 prevents a 2 × 2 inverse

Main idea

Construct a nonzero vector sent to zero. Handle zero first-row entries separately, so no case is silently lost.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Why ad - bc = 0 prevents a 2 × 2 inverse.

Words used in this question

Homogeneous means the right side is the zero vector. The zero input always works; nontrivial means a different, nonzero input.

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

  1. If

    (a,b)≠(0,0)(a,b) ≠ (0,0)

    , let

    x=(−b,a)x = (-b,a)

  2. It is nonzero and Ax = (-ab + ba,-cb + da) = (0,ad - bc) = 0.

  3. If

    a=b=0a = b = 0

    but

    (c,d)≠(0,0)(c,d) ≠ (0,0)

    , choose

    x=(−d,c)x = (-d,c)

  4. both row products are zero and x is nonzero.

  5. If all entries are zero, choose

    x=(1,0)x = (1,0)

  6. Thus every case supplies a nontrivial homogeneous solution in addition to

    x=0x = 0

  7. An inverse would force every such solution to zero by left multiplication, a contradiction.

FINAL ANSWER

There is a nonzero solution of Ax = 0 in every case, so A cannot be invertible.

exercises.title: Prove the 2 × 2 formula works
exercises.question: Prove Theorem 4 for A = [abcd][a,b;c,d].
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Given

δ = ad − bc is nonzero.

What must be shown

Prove the 2 × 2 formula works

Main idea

Multiply the proposed inverse in both orders. The off-diagonal terms cancel and the diagonal entries become δ/δ.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Prove the 2 × 2 formula works.

Words used in this question

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

  1. Put

    δ=ad−bc≠0δ = ad - bc ≠ 0

    and

    C=(1δ)[d−b−ca]C = (1/δ)[d,-b;-c,a]

  2. Then AC = (1/δ)[ad−bc−ab+bacd−dc−cb+da][ad - bc,-ab + ba;cd - dc,-cb + da] = I2I₂.

  3. Likewise CA = (1/δ)[da−bcdb−bd−ca+ac−cb+ad][da - bc,db - bd;-ca + ac,-cb + ad] = I2I₂.

  4. Division is permitted because δ is nonzero.

  5. Both inverse identities hold, proving

    C=A−1C = A^(-1)

    by definition.

FINAL ANSWER

The proposed matrix C is A−1A⁻¹ because AC = CA = I2I₂ and the nonzero determinant makes every division valid.

exercises.title: Show row operations equal elementary left products
exercises.question: Prove these special cases of the elementary-matrix facts. Here A is a 3 × 3 matrix and I = I3I₃. A general proof would require more notation.
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Given

A is 3 × 3, I = I3I₃, and E comes from the stated operation on I.

What must be shown

Show row operations equal elementary left products

Main idea

A row of I selects one row of A. Changing that selector row performs the same operation on the product EA.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Show row operations equal elementary left products.

  1. Part (a): row i of I selects row i of A in the product,

  2. so rowiw_i(I)A = rowiw_i(A).

  3. Part (b): swapping rows 1 and 2 of I3I₃ gives

    E=[010100001]E = [0,1,0;1,0,0;0,0,1]

  4. Its first row selects row 2 of A, second selects row 1, third selects row 3;

  5. therefore EA performs the stated interchange.

  6. Part (c):

    E=diag (1,1,5)E = diag(1,1,5)

    has third row 5row3w₃(I),

  7. so row 3 of EA is 5row3w₃(A), with the other rows unchanged.

  8. Each claim follows from the same row-column rule, for arbitrary entries of A.

FINAL ANSWER

Each of the stated row operations equals left multiplication by the elementary matrix obtained by doing the same operation on I3I₃.

exercises.title: Elementary matrix for row 3 minus four times row 1
exercises.question: Prove these special cases of the elementary-matrix facts. Here A is a 3 × 3 matrix and I = I3I₃. A general proof would require more notation.
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Given

A is 3 × 3; replace row 3 by row 3 minus four copies of row 1.

What must be shown

Elementary matrix for row 3 minus four times row 1

Main idea

Make the same change in I3I₃. Its new third row then selects row 3 of A minus four copies of row 1.

Proof steps and justification

Your task. Elementary matrix for row 3 minus four times row 1.

Words used in this question

A coefficient is the number multiplying an unknown. A missing term has coefficient 0.

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

  1. Take

    E=[100010−401]E = [1,0,0;0,1,0;-4,0,1]

    , obtained by that operation on I3I₃.

  2. The first two rows of EA reproduce rows 1 and 2 of A.

  3. Its third row is -4row1w₁(A) + row3w₃(A), since E’s third-row coefficients are -4,0,1.

  4. Thus EA is exactly the requested row replacement.

  5. Its inverse adds four times row 1 to row 3, confirming reversibility.

FINAL ANSWER

Use E = [100010−401][1,0,0;0,1,0;−4,0,1]. Its third row of EA is row3w₃(A) − 4row1w₁(A), with the other rows unchanged.

exercises.title: Inverse of the lower-triangular matrix with column weights
exercises.question: Given in Exercise 2.2.43
exercises.solution:
Independently derived teaching solution; no matching selected answer is present on Combined PDF pages 101-116.

Your task. Inverse of the lower-triangular matrix with column weights.

Words used in this question

An inverse undoes a square matrix: both multiplication orders must give the identity. The identity has diagonal 1s and all other entries 0.

See the pattern first for n = 3

The diagonal contains positions (i,i). The subdiagonal is immediately below it, at positions (i,i−1).

Separate the triangular pattern from the column weights

A=LDA = LD

Right multiplication by D scales column j of L by j, which reconstructs A.

Undo those actions in reverse order

A−1=D−1L−1A^(-1) = D^(-1)L^(-1)

L−1L⁻¹ subtracts the preceding row; D−1D⁻¹ divides row i by i. All divisors i are nonzero positive integers.

State the general candidate precisely

Bii=1iB_{ii} = 1/i
Bi,i−1=−1iB_{i,i-1} = -1/i

The second formula applies for i ≥ 2. All other entries are zero.

Verify BA by subtracting two actual rows

(row i(A)−row i−1(A))i=eiT(row_i(A) - row_{i-1}(A))/i = e_i^T

For i ≥ 2, the first i−1 entries cancel. The surviving entry is i in position i; division by i makes it 1. Row 1 of A is already e1Te₁ᵀ. Hence every row of BA is the matching identity row.

Verify AB by its entries

j(1j)=1j(1/j) = 1

This is the diagonal case. Below the diagonal the only two possible contributions cancel:

j(1j)+(j+1)(−1j+1)=1−1=0j(1/j) + (j+1)(-1/(j+1)) = 1 - 1 = 0

Above the diagonal every contribution is zero. Thus AB also equals I.

FINAL ANSWER

The inverse has diagonal entry 1/i, subdiagonal entry −1/i, and zeros elsewhere, with the subdiagonal rule used for i ≥ 2. Both inverse identities have been verified.

MATH 2255 - Complete Exercise Workbook and Worked Solutions

Companion to Linear Algebra Made Understandable

This volume preserves the supplied exercise pages, organized by section, and gives a numbered answer for each complete visible question. Original question numbers are retained, including all visible subparts. The source is Exercises_Merged.pdf (16 physical PDF pages). Selected course solutions are from physical pages 101-116 of Heli-exampm_prep_Combined.pdf.

Coverage boundary. There are 337 complete numbered questions and two cut-off numbered questions in the supplied scans. The incomplete entries are 1.2.41 and 2.1.43; their missing continuations are identified at their positions. Printed directions also mention 1.4.33-34 and 1.9.31-32, whose actual statements are absent. No unseen continuation or absent statement is invented. Exercise 2.1.14 refers to a cost matrix in an example not supplied; its requested structural interpretation can still be fully answered from the description in the question.

Computations and proofs here are independently written teaching solutions. A source cross-check label means the matching supplied selected solution was used to validate the result, not that all wording or steps are official. Full row reductions may choose different valid operations from those shown in the source. Exact fractions are retained. For parametric answers, different symbols or nonzero rescalings of directions may describe the same set.

Reading the worked solutions

The original scans supply the question statements. The answers restate the mathematical task and then explain the method. The displayed matrices after row operations are full updated matrices, not unrecorded leaps. After a reduction, the answer translates the rows into equations, identifies the free choices, and verifies against the original entries. For independence, the unknowns are the weights of the vectors. For a range or span question, the unknowns are weights producing the target output.

When an exercise asks only for existence, an answer may show more reduction than strictly necessary to make the reasoning self-contained. You may stop a hand calculation once a contradiction or the required pivot information is established. When an exercise asks for no full solution, its answer below stops at that decision and explains why it is sufficient.

Proof answers state the assumptions and connect them with the definitions. A false universal statement is accompanied by an explicit counterexample or a precise failure of its definition. A true/false label by itself is never the justification.
